title: OpenFOAM: fluid steps as OpenFOAM cases, and results read back (finishing #950)
solver: Lanczos returns unconverged Ritz pairs when its basis budget runs out or the next block does not fit
body:
### Observed failure

`eigen::lanczos` sets `full = m >= max_basis || m + b > n` and then treats `full` as the Krylov space being exhausted: the residual bound of every Ritz pair is taken as zero (`if !full { … }`, and `if full { 0.0 }` for the negative ones). The space is exhausted only when `m >= n`. When the budget runs out (`m >= max_basis`), or the next block does not fit (`m + b > n` with `m < n`), the returned eigenvalues and vectors can be far from converged, and no error says so.

### Reproduction

With the cavity step of #1081 (the frequency and buckling steps call the same function):

1. A box of 2 × 1 × 2 Kuhn cells, 1 × 0.5 × 0.75 m, every wall a conductor, order 1, 4 modes. It has nine free edges. Lanczos stops at six vectors (`6 + 6 > 9`) and returns 256, 421, 439 and 487 MHz under the default limits. Its missed-mode check (an LDLᵀ inertia count) warns that 5 modes lie below 487 MHz and 3 were found, so the values are not the eigenvalues of the discrete problem.
2. A finer box (4 × 2 × 3 cells), 2 modes above a `min_hz` between its first and second modes, with `max_lanczos_vectors: 6`: it returns 501.6 and 582.5 MHz without an error, and the inertia count finds 19 modes between the bound and 582.5 MHz where one was returned. Under the default limits the same step returns the full solve's second and third modes.

Found by CodeRabbit's review of #1081 (crates/solver/src/cavity.rs:599).

### Evidence

`crates/solver/src/eigen.rs` (at 655d92fe):

```rust
let full = m >= max_basis || m + b > n;
…
if !full {
    for r in 0..b { … res2 += v * v; }  // residual skipped when full
}
…
if full && !done {
    if m >= n { done = true; } else { return Err(NotConverged(…)) }
}
```

`done` is reached with `found == wanted.count` even when the residuals were skipped. So the `NotConverged` branch catches only the case where too few Ritz values lie in the band.

### Expected behaviour

A Ritz pair is returned only when its residual bound passes, unless the basis spans the whole space (`m >= n`), where Ritz pairs are exact. At the budget, the pairs that pass are kept, and the step fails with `NotConverged` (or reports a shortfall) when the requested ones do not.

### Investigation

- At the budget or a short last block, the residual can still be bounded without the next block's QR factor: ‖W s_last‖ in the M-norm, with W the block before `orthonormalize`.
- When `m + b > n`, a last block of `n − m` vectors would reach `m = n`, where every Ritz pair is exact. This makes small problems (fewer than two blocks of unknowns) exact.
- Callers: `analysis.rs` (frequency), `buckle.rs` (both shifts), `cavity.rs`. #1081 adds an inertia check to the cavity step for the `min_hz` case as well, so a cavity step warns when this happens, but the frequency step has no such check.
- A regression test: a problem with `n` between `b` and `2b`, and one at `max_lanczos_vectors: b`, where the converged and the returned values differ.

### Version and platform

Linux. `eigen.rs` as on develop at 655d92fe (last changed in 533a4b49).

title: results.path fails with "path point location remains unresolved" inside undistorted tet10 blocks and on some tet4 surface points
body: ### Observed failure `results.path` fails for the whole path, on straight, undistorted elements made by `mesh.block`: ``` `points` element 4: invalid input: path point location remains unresolved after bounded inverse/subdivision search; refine the distorted element or move the path ``` - **tet10:** most stations inside the block fail, so in practice no path can be sampled on a tet10 mesh. - **tet4:** stations inside the block work, but some on the outer surface fail. The Path Plot panel's surface picking lands on such points, so picking two points on a face and pressing **Sample path** fails too. None of these elements is distorted (the tet10 mid-side nodes sit exactly at the edge midpoints), so the hint in the message does not apply. ### Reproduction `fieldcraft-cli run repro.json` with a free frequency step on a 1000 × 500 × 750 mm block, 2 × 1 × 2 divisions: ```json [ {"command": "mesh.block", "params": {"body": "Box", "kind": "tet10", "divisions": [2, 1, 2], "corners": [[0,0,0],[1000,0,0],[1000,500,0],[0,500,0],[0,0,750],[1000,0,750],[1000,500,750],[0,500,750]]}}, {"command": "model.set.create", "params": {"name": "all", "geometry": [{"body": "Box"}]}}, {"command": "model.material.create", "params": {"name": "Mat", "elastic": {"type": "isotropic", "young": 1000, "poisson": 0}, "density": 1}}, {"command": "model.section.create", "params": {"name": "s", "set": "all", "material": "Mat", "kind": {"type": "solid"}}}, {"command": "model.step.create", "params": {"name": "Modes", "procedure": {"type": "frequency", "modes": 7}}}, {"command": "solve.frequency", "params": {}}, {"command": "results.path", "params": {"step": "Modes", "field": "displacement", "mode": 7, "samples": 11, "points": [[100, 250, 300], [900, 250, 300]]}} ] ``` ``` error: step 7 (results.path): `points` element 4: invalid input: path point location remains unresolved … ``` Two-station paths (`samples: 2`) from each point below to the same point moved 0.001 mm in x isolate single points: | Mesh | Point (mm) | Result | |---|---|---| | tet10 | `[100, 250, 300]` | fails, element 4 | | tet10 | `[100, 100, 100]` | fails, element 2 | | tet10 | `[700, 300, 500]` | fails, element 19 | | tet10 | `[250, 250, 187.5]` | value | | tet4 | `[899, 0, 300]` | fails, element 8 | | tet4 | `[900, 0, 300.00007]` | fails, element 8 | | tet4 | `[900, 0, 300]`, `[880, 0, 300]`, `[900, 1, 300]` | value | | tet4 | `[100, 250, 300]` → `[900, 250, 300]`, 11 and 101 samples | values | The tet4 points are on the face y = 0, on the block's outer surface. In the app: open Path Plot on the solved step, tick **Pick surface points**, click two points on the front face near (100, 0, 300) and (900, 0, 300) mm, and press **Sample path**. It fails on both meshes (tet10 at element 2, tet4 at element 8). The same picked coordinates sent as `results.path` fail in the same way, so the panel is not the cause. ### Evidence Element 4 of the tet10 block (m) is a valid straight tet10: ``` corners [0,0,0] [0,0.5,0] [0,0.5,0.375] [0.5,0.5,0.375] midsides [0,0.25,0] [0,0.5,0.1875] [0,0.25,0.1875] [0.25,0.25,0.1875] [0.25,0.5,0.1875] [0.25,0.5,0.375] ``` Each mid-side node is its edge's midpoint (`ElementKind::Tet10.edges()` order). tet10, Path Plot after **Sample path** on two picked surface points: tet4, the same: ### Expected behaviour A value at every station inside the block or on its surface, and `null` only outside the mesh, on both tet4 and tet10. ### Investigation Not settled. `results.path` asks every candidate element whose bounds hold the station, in label order (`engine/src/path.rs`, `Index::find`), and `fieldcraft_fem::locate` must either locate the station in it or prove it outside. For the failing elements, Newton from the centre and the four corner-weighted seeds gives no inside point, and `exclude` (the interval subdivision) then cannot prove the station outside, so the whole path errors instead of moving to the next candidate. - For tet4 and straight tet10 the map is affine, so the natural coordinates are exact and the outside proof should be immediate. That it is not suggests the interval enclosure in `exclude` is not tight for these kinds, or does not get the nodes in the order `interval_weights` expects for tet10. - The tet4 failures are stations on the plane of a face of a neighbouring candidate, where an outside proof needs exact or tightly enclosed arithmetic. No test in `crates/engine` runs `results.path` on tet10 or at surface stations today; found while adding mid-side fields to cavity results (#1081). ### Version and platform Linux, 0.8.1. Run on the #1081 branch (based on develop at 655d92fe), which does not change `fieldcraft_fem::locate`, `engine/src/path.rs` or the Path Plot panel.

title: Panels: pop out panels to native desktop windows and drag out of the app (SolidCraft parity)
body:
### Current behaviour

All desktop panels (Browser, Context / Command forms, History, Results / Path panels) are rendered inside the single main window over the viewport via `crates/ui-egui/src/shell.rs`. There is no way to pop a panel out into its own native OS window or drag it onto a second monitor.

### What you need and why

During post-processing and complex model inspection (e.g. viewing results plots, path plots, fracture/XY charts, or inspecting model definitions alongside a 3D mesh), engineers often want the 3D viewport unobstructed on one monitor while keeping charts, tables, or inspector panels open on a second monitor.

Now that `crates/ui-egui` uses `solidcraft-ui-kit` and mirrors SolidCraft's `shell.rs` card layout, bringing SolidCraft's shared panel-host / pop-out / drag-out workflow to FieldCraft would also keep the two Craft-family desktop apps consistent.

### Expected behaviour

On desktop, supported panels (e.g. Browser, History, Results / Path panels, and future analysis panels) can be:
1. Popped out into their own native OS window via **Pop out to window** (closing the window docks the panel back where it was, keeping drafts, selection, and open state intact).
2. Dragged by their title bar outside the main app window onto another screen, opening directly as that same native window (matching `tangency-labs/solidcraft#16216`).
3. Kept inside the main window on `wasm32` / headless `ui.capture` / `--control` runs, or when the platform does not report window position.

**Questions before I start a PR series:**
1. Is this a direction you want in `tangency-labs/fieldcraft`?
2. Should the shared `panel_runtime` / pop-out host be **lifted into `solidcraft-ui-kit`** (or another shared crate) so SolidCraft and FieldCraft share one implementation, or **adapted into `crates/ui-egui`** (credited in `ATTRIBUTION.md`)?
3. Would you prefer this split as a small sequential PR series (e.g., PR 1: panel host + docking over `shell.rs`; PR 2: native **Pop out to window** + `wasm32`/headless fallback; PR 3: drag-out outside the app window)?

### Pictures

See the before/after captures in `tangency-labs/solidcraft#16216` showing Browser and History dragged out of the main window into native OS windows.

### References

- `tangency-labs/solidcraft#16216` — *Panels: drag any panel out of the app into its own window*
- Prerequisite SolidCraft PRs referenced there: `#11218` (shared panel host), `#11308`, `#15210`, `#20479` (pop-out windows)

title: Import follow-ups from #1052's review: v3 fixtures in the real-file tests, hostile-test causes, glTF warning match
body:
Follow-ups from the independent review of #1052 (import, B-rep-only meshing). None blocks the merge.

1. **The v3 fixtures skip two required file tests.** They aren't in the real-file tests docs/formats/fieldcraft.md requires: the step-only check and the bit-identical save and reopen. `crates/io/tests/formats.rs:431-520` still loops over `fixtures(1)` only. Extend it to `fixtures(3)`.
2. **The OBJ and PLY hostile tests check failure, not its cause.** `cut_obj` and `bad_ply_face` only assert that the import fails (`crates/geometry/src/triangles.rs:333-334, 368-371`), not that it fails because the reader left geometry out. Assert the message.
3. **`NOTHING_LEFT_OUT` matches SolidCraft's message wording** (`triangles.rs:52`). That fails safe, but a reworded SolidCraft message would start refusing good glTF files, and no textured-glTF test would catch it. Add a textured glTF that must import, or ask SolidCraft for a structured "left out" count on the import feature instead of message text.
4. **No test opens an FCStd or 3dm file:** the pinned SolidCraft can't write either format. Add one once it can, or once a small public-domain sample is available.

title: RFC 0001: edges and faces in the DofLayout, Nédélec elements and the cavity step (phases 1 and 2)
body:
### Current behaviour

Since #1037 the solver factors complex-symmetric matrices, but FieldCraft has no element for the electric field and the degree-of-freedom layout numbers nodes only (docs/rfc/0001-electromagnetics.md §2, §3.1).

### What you need and why

The rest of phase 1 (the entity-keyed `DofLayout`, which jyviko handed over on Discord) and phase 2 of RFC 0001 (#971): Nédélec elements, perfect conductors and the cavity eigen step, checked against the cases of RFC §4.

### Expected behaviour

Three pull requests, each on the one before:

1. **`fem`: the layout numbers mesh edges and faces.** A slot is an `Entity` (node, edge, face, point); edges and faces come after the nodes, by their sorted labels, each entity's unknowns contiguous, so `NodeGraph`, `add_block` and the ordering work on them unchanged. Two unknown kinds, `E1` and `E2`. A layout without edges and faces is the one it was.
2. **`fem`: Nédélec tetrahedra of orders 1 and 2** (Whitney; Webb's hierarchical basis), built on corners sorted by label (RFC §8.1), declaring their edges and faces to the layout, with the discrete gradient G (RFC §8.2). A rectangular cavity assembled through the layout as a solver test.
3. **The cavity step end to end**: εᵣ and μᵣ on materials, a `perfect_conductor` boundary condition on faces, a `cavity` step, `solve.cavity` with the null space projected out (RFC §8.4) and the LDLᵀ inertia as a check for missed modes, the electric field in the results.

### Pictures

_No response_

### References

- J.-C. Nédélec, Numer. Math. 35:315–341, 1980; J. P. Webb, IEEE Trans. Antennas Propag. 47(8):1244–1253, 1999.
- P. Arbenz, R. Geus, Appl. Numer. Math. 54(2):107–121, 2005 (the null-space projection).
- D. M. Pozar, *Microwave Engineering*, 4th ed., 2012, §6.4; R. F. Harrington, *Time-Harmonic Electromagnetic Fields*, 1961, ch. 4; D. Boffi, Acta Numer. 19:1–120, 2010.

title: shells: MITC4 is 74 % too stiff on the MacNeal–Harder twisted beam (warped elements, 12 × 2)
body:
### Observed failure

The MacNeal–Harder twisted beam (L = 12, width 1.1, thickness 0.32, 90° pretwist, E = 29 × 10⁶, ν = 0.22, clamped root, unit tip force spread as consistent nodal loads over the tip edge) built with quad4 (MITC4) shells, mesh written node by node (#1066), is far too stiff on the prescribed 12 × 2 mesh and converges slowly:

| mesh | in-plane u_z (ref 0.005424) | out-of-plane u_y (ref 0.001754) |
|---|---|---|
| 12 × 2 | 0.0013905 (−74.4 %) | 7.3719 × 10⁻⁴ (−58.0 %) |
| 24 × 4 | 0.0029356 (−45.9 %) | 0.0010950 (−37.6 %) |
| 48 × 8 | 0.0045010 (−17.0 %) | 0.0015057 (−14.2 %) |
| 96 × 16 | 0.0052691 (−2.85 %) | 0.0017104 (−2.49 %) |

The references check against beam theory with the section's principal compliance turning along the span: δ = (P/E) ∫ (L − x)² [cos²θ/I_t + sin²θ/I_w] dx = 5.426 × 10⁻³ (in-plane) and 1.745 × 10⁻³ (out-of-plane), so the model and the loads are right. MacNeal and Harder report that quadrilateral shells pass this test within a few per cent on 12 × 2. Errors of this size that shrink by a factor of 2 to 6 per refinement are locking, not the mesh error of a shell element.

### Expected behaviour

Within 2 % of the reference on 12 × 2 (MacNeal–Harder grade A), or a documented, cited limitation of flat-facet elements on warped geometry.

### Suspected cause (to confirm)

Each element is projected onto its mean plane (elements.md, Shells: "the facet approach"). The 12 × 2 elements are warped (7.5° twist per element), and the projection without a warping correction (rigid links from the nodes to the flat facet) leaves the warped element's nodes off its plane.

### References

- R. H. MacNeal, R. L. Harder, FEAD 1 (1985) 3–20, Fig. 6, Table 3.
- R. L. Taylor, *Finite element analysis of linear shell problems*, in The Mathematics of Finite Elements and Applications VI, 1987 (warping correction of flat elements).
- E. N. Dvorkin, K.-J. Bathe, Engineering Computations 1 (1984) 77–88 (MITC4 on warped geometry).

title: loads: a temperature load that varies in space (activates NAFEMS LE11)
body:
### Current behaviour

The oracle case `nafems-le11` is pending: it needs the temperature field T = (x² + y²)^½ + z (°C) on the nodes of a static step. A static step's `temperature` load sets one value on a target (docs/manual/structural/linear-static.md, Loads), so a field that varies over the part can only come from a coupled step's conduction solution or an initial field mapped from another model; T = r + z is not a conduction solution (∇²T = 1/r).

### What you need and why

NAFEMS LE11 is the standard linear thermal-stress benchmark (target σ_zz = −105 MPa at A); the thermal strain of solids is already implemented, only the field input is missing.

### Expected behaviour

- A temperature load whose value varies in space. Maintainer's choice: an expression of x, y, z (the form other loads would share, cf. #981 spatially varying pressure) or a per-node table.
- nafems-le11 activated with its tolerance and refinement, docs/oracle.md regenerated.

### References

- NAFEMS, *The Standard NAFEMS Benchmarks*, TNSB Rev. 3, 1990, test LE11.

title: elements: axisymmetric shells (two-node conical frustum); fixes the nafems-le7 known failure
body:
### Current behaviour

There is no axisymmetric shell. The oracle case `nafems-le7` is a known failure for that reason: its target is the axisymmetric thin-shell solution and our axisymmetric solid model converges to 25.27 (−2.2 %).

### What you need and why

M4's element library (2D, #30 plan: "Axisymmetric shells (2-node, 3-node)"): tanks, domes and pressure vessels in 2D axisymmetric models.

### Expected behaviour

- A two-node conical-frustum shell in the axisymmetric half plane (u_r, u_z, θ) beside axisymmetric continua. Maintainer's choice of formulation: the Kirchhoff frustum (Grafton & Strome 1963) or a shear-deformable frustum with one-point shear integration (Zienkiewicz, Taylor & Fox 2014, ch. on axisymmetric shells).
- Verified by a closed thin cylinder and a sphere under pressure (membrane closed forms), a cylinder edge bending (Timoshenko & Woinowsky-Krieger, the decay length), and nafems-le7.

### References

- P. E. Grafton, D. R. Strome, *Analysis of axisymmetrical shells by the direct stiffness method*, AIAA J. 1 (1963) 2342–2347.
- O. C. Zienkiewicz, R. L. Taylor, D. Fox, *The Finite Element Method for Solid and Structural Mechanics*, 7th ed., 2014.
- S. Timoshenko, S. Woinowsky-Krieger, *Theory of Plates and Shells*, 2nd ed., 1959.

title: elements: axisymmetric elements with twist
body:
### Current behaviour

Axisymmetric elements carry u_r and u_z only. elements.md lists axisymmetric elements with twist as not implemented.

### What you need and why

M4's element library (2D, #30 plan): revolved parts under torsion (shafts, couplings) analysed on their meridian section.

### Expected behaviour

- Axisymmetric elements with twist: a third unknown u_θ per node with the shear strains γ_rθ = ∂u_θ/∂r − u_θ/r and γ_zθ = ∂u_θ/∂z, tri3/tri6/quad4/quad8, torque loads; static and frequency.
- Verified by a solid and a hollow shaft in torsion (Saint-Venant: exact rotation and τ = T r / J) and a stepped shaft against its closed form.

### References

- O. C. Zienkiewicz, R. L. Taylor, J. Z. Zhu, 2013, ch. 9 (axisymmetric problems).
- S. P. Timoshenko, J. N. Goodier, *Theory of Elasticity*, 1970, ch. 10 (torsion of shafts of variable diameter).

title: elements: generalized plane strain
body:
### Current behaviour

2D continua are plane stress, plane strain (ε_zz = 0) or axisymmetric. elements.md lists generalized plane strain as not implemented.

### What you need and why

M4's element library (2D, #30 plan): long prismatic parts whose ends are free to extend (thermal or axial loads), where plane strain over-constrains ε_zz.

### Expected behaviour

- Generalized plane strain: the out-of-plane strain is a global unknown, ε_zz = ε₀ (+ κ_x y − κ_y x if the bending curvatures are included), held by a reference point that also takes the axial force (and moments).
- Maintainer's choice: ε₀ only, or ε₀ and the two curvatures.
- Verified by a free long cylinder heated uniformly or under axial force (exact uniaxial ε_zz), and the thick cylinder with closed ends (Lamé with the end-cap force).

### References

- O. C. Zienkiewicz, R. L. Taylor, J. Z. Zhu, *The Finite Element Method: Its Basis and Fundamentals*, 7th ed., 2013.
- S. P. Timoshenko, J. N. Goodier, *Theory of Elasticity*, 3rd ed., 1970 (closed-end thick cylinder).

title: elements: pipe elements with internal pressure (elbows later)
body:
### Current behaviour

A pipe is a beam with a `pipe` profile: no internal pressure, no hoop stress, no elbows. elements.md lists pipe and elbow elements as not implemented.

### What you need and why

M4's element library ("Pipe / elbow" in the #30 plan): piping systems under internal pressure.

### Expected behaviour

- A pipe element: the beam with a pipe profile plus internal (and external) pressure, giving the end-cap axial force, hoop and radial stresses through the wall (Lamé) and the Bourdon effect of curved pipes left to the elbow.
- Elbow ovalisation (von Kármán flexibility factors) as a second step, on its own issue.
- Verified by a closed pipe under pressure (Lamé thick-wall and thin-wall hoop stress) and a pressurised pipe loop's deflection.

### References

- S. P. Timoshenko, J. N. Goodier, *Theory of Elasticity*, 3rd ed., 1970 (Lamé).
- T. von Kármán, *Über die Formänderung dünnwandiger Rohre*, VDI 55 (1911) 1889–1895 (elbow flexibility).

title: elements: planar beams in 2D models (u_x, u_y, θ_z)
body:
### Current behaviour

A 2D model (plane stress, plane strain) takes trusses but no beams (elements.md: "A 2D model takes no couplings, no shells or beams").

### What you need and why

M4's element library ("Beam, 2D (planar frames)" in the #30 plan): in-plane frames and stiffeners in 2D models, three unknowns per node (u_x, u_y, θ_z).

### Expected behaviour

- The existing Timoshenko beam restricted to the XY plane (axial, one bending plane), its nodes carrying Ux, Uy, Rz, sharing nodes with 2D continua and trusses; static and frequency; Abaqus planar beam, Nastran and LS-DYNA by their 3D elements held in the plane or refused by name.
- Verified by a planar portal frame (slope-deflection), a cantilever tip load (exact) and a plane frame's first frequency.

### References

- J. S. Przemieniecki, *Theory of Matrix Structural Analysis*, 1968, ch. 5.
- Z. Friedman, J. B. Kosmatka, *An improved two-node Timoshenko beam finite element*, Computers & Structures 47 (1993) 473–481.

title: elements: three-node (quadratic) Timoshenko beam, straight or curved
body:
### Current behaviour

Beams are two-node and straight. elements.md lists the three-node beam as not implemented.

### What you need and why

M4's element library ("1D elements II" in the #30 plan): curved and stocky members, and a quadratic beam to sit on the mid-side nodes of quadratic solid and shell meshes.

### Expected behaviour

- A three-node (quadratic) Timoshenko beam, straight or curved, with the six unknowns per node of the existing beam, in static and frequency steps and the decks.
- The formulation is a choice for the maintainer between published ones: reduced (two-point) integration of the shear and membrane terms (Prathap & Bhashyam 1982; Stolarski & Belytschko 1982) or assumed (substitute) shear strain fields (MacNeal 1978; Bathe 2014 §5.4).
- Verified by a curved cantilever (closed form), a quarter ring under a radial load and convergence rates.

### References

- G. Prathap, G. R. Bhashyam, *Reduced integration and the shear-flexible beam element*, IJNME 18 (1982) 195–210.
- H. Stolarski, T. Belytschko, *Membrane locking and reduced integration for curved elements*, J. Appl. Mech. 49 (1982) 172–176.
- K.-J. Bathe, *Finite Element Procedures*, 2nd ed., 2014, §5.4.

title: elements: Euler–Bernoulli (cubic) two-node beam
body:
### Current behaviour

The only beam is the two-node Timoshenko beam (`crates/fem/src/beam.rs`, interdependent interpolation with Φ = 12 EI/(G A_s L²)). docs/manual/structural/elements.md (Limitations) lists the Euler–Bernoulli (cubic) beam as not implemented.

### What you need and why

M4's element library (ROADMAP: "Element library per elements.md, 1D and 2D first"; the family plan of #30, "1D elements II"). Slender frames are analysed with shear-rigid beams, and the deck writers need the shear-rigid element to map to each solver's cubic beam.

### Expected behaviour

- A beam section without transverse shear flexibility: the Hermite cubic element, the Φ → 0 limit of the existing kernel (Przemieniecki 1968, §5.6), in static, frequency and the decks (Abaqus cubic beam, Nastran beam without shear flexibility, LS-DYNA counterpart or a refusal by name).
- Verified by exact end-load deflections, a portal frame (slope-deflection without shear) and the Euler–Bernoulli frequencies of a cantilever.

### References

- J. S. Przemieniecki, *Theory of Matrix Structural Analysis*, McGraw-Hill, 1968, §5.6.
- R. D. Cook et al., *Concepts and Applications of Finite Element Analysis*, 4th ed., 2002, ch. 2.

title: oracle: MacNeal–Harder twisted beam and pinched hemisphere shell benchmarks (pending cases)
body:
### Current behaviour

Two shell benchmarks of MacNeal and Harder (1985) wait in `tests/oracle/` as pending cases: `mh-twisted-beam` and `pinched-hemisphere`. Their `expected.json` already cites the reference values (0.005424 and 0.001754 for the twisted beam, 0.0940 for the hemisphere); they say they need a doubly curved or helical shell mesh. `scordelis-lo-roof-shell` and `pinched-cylinder` show that such a mesh can be written node by node with `mesh.node.add` and `mesh.element.add`, the route docs/verification.md allows.

### What you need and why

M4 lists the MITC4/MITC3 shells as done, verified by Scordelis–Lo and the pinched cylinder. The twisted beam (warped elements) and the pinched hemisphere (doubly curved, inextensional bending) are the two remaining standard shell tests of the same source; they are the cases a flat-facet MITC4 is most likely to miss.

### Expected behaviour

- Both cases get a recipe (nodes and quad4 elements written one by one, generator script in the README), a measure, a tolerance with its reason, and a refinement table.
- A result inside the tolerance is blessed; a result outside it is recorded as a known failure with its cause, never by widening the tolerance.
- docs/oracle.md regenerated in the commit that activates each case.

### References

- R. H. MacNeal, R. L. Harder, *A proposed standard set of problems to test finite element accuracy*, FEAD 1 (1985) 3–20, Fig. 6 / Table 3 (twisted beam), Fig. 9 / Table 5(b) (hemisphere).
- T. Belytschko et al., *Stress projection for membrane and shear locking in shell finite elements*, CMAME 51 (1985) 221–258.

title: EM phase 1: entity-keyed DofLayout (edges and faces), RFC 0001 §3.1/§8
body:
### Current behaviour

RFC 0001 (electromagnetics), phase 1, has two halves. The complex half is merged (#1037): `Csr`, assembly and LDLᵀ are generic over `f64` and `Complex64`, and the f64 path is unchanged bit for bit. The other half isn't started: `crates/fem/src/dof.rs` `DofLayout` numbers unknowns per node only. Edge elements (phase 2) need unknowns on edges and faces.

### Expected behaviour

An entity-keyed `DofLayout`, as RFC 0001 §3.1 proposes and §8 details. Open question 1 is decided as the RFC proposes: one layout keyed by entity, not a separate edge layout, so constraints, results and the control channel see a single numbering. §8.2 adds the port-mode problem as a further reason.

- **Tables:** global edge and face tables of the tetrahedra, numbered after the nodes in a fixed order from sorted vertex labels (determinism).
- **Orientation:** elements get their vertices' sort permutation, not a sign per entity (§8.1).
- **Functions:** counts per entity by kind, sized for order 2, with the Whitney and gradient slots of an edge named.
- **Boundaries:** lookup by element face (an edge is held when a face containing it is held, never by its end nodes).
- **Discrete gradient:** G, with the test K G = 0 to rounding.
- **Mixed unknowns:** nodal and edge unknowns in one system; entities without unknowns, and unknowns on part of the mesh.
- **Pattern and ordering by entity:** the graph is generalised from nodes to entities, with a point per entity (edge midpoint, face centroid). An entity's unknowns stay contiguous.
- **The structural path must not change:** a node-only layout gives the same numbering, pattern, ordering and results bit for bit, checked by the existing structural freeze and oracle.

Tests as §3.1 and §8.1 name them: a constant-curl field reproduced, and tangential continuity at order 2 on a face shared by two tets that see it in different vertex orders.

title: lbm: TRT grows about a uniform stream at the laminar floor (τ⁺ 0.505, oblique, U 0.05)
body:
### Current behaviour

Found while bounding the MRT collision for #1057 (notes: swarm board `lbm-dd/notes/expert-mrt-bound.md`). A von Neumann analysis of the TRT collision, about a uniform stream at lattice velocity 0.05 in an oblique direction, finds a growing wave at τ⁺ = 0.505, the laminar floor: growth of about 6e-3 per step. TRT is the collision #1057's refusal of sub-bound MRT points users away from, along with regularized and HRR.

### Expected behaviour

- **Bound:** establish TRT's linear stability bound about a uniform stream, as a function of τ⁺, the magic parameter Λ and lattice Mach, against the published TRT stability analyses (e.g. Kuzmin, Ginzburg & Mohamad 2011).
- **Floor:** state whether `MIN_TAU` 0.505 is inside it.
- **If it isn't:** refuse or warn on TRT where it is unstable, as #1057 does for MRT, and record it in the collision docs.

title: lbm: MIN_LINK_FRACTION 0.01 clamps q near 0 and costs interpolated walls an order (1.72 vs 2.00)
body:
### Current behaviour

`MIN_LINK_FRACTION = 0.01` (`crates/lbm/src/voxel.rs:315, 338`) clamps an interpolated wall link's fraction q from below. A link whose true crossing is at or near its fluid node (q ≈ 0) is treated as q = 0.01. For walls passing through, or very near, cell centres, that adds an error that falls only as 1/N, a first-order term in a second-order method.

Measured while finishing #1001 (expert notes: swarm board `lbm-dd/expert-1001.md`). Rotated Poiseuille channel at 45°, whole-row widths, quadratic interpolated walls (Bouzidi, Firdaouss & Lallemand 2001); observed L2 order with the wall at offset ±1e-6 cells:

| | with the floor | without |
|---|---|---|
| quadratic | 1.72 | 2.00 |

The floor held 308, 644 and 1256 links on the 8-, 16- and 24-cell grids. The 2:1-slope case at offset 0.67 (order 1.78) probably has the same cause, with q ≈ 0.001. The linear rule on develop shares the floor.

### Expected behaviour

- Remove the floor, or derive it: Bouzidi's linear and quadratic rules are defined at q = 0, where the wall is on the fluid node.
- Show that q → 0 is safe: no division by q in either rule, and the q < ½ branch coefficients bounded.
- Re-record what moves in the interpolated-wall tests and the oracle, each change justified against the exact solution.
- The order study checks second order with the wall exactly at a node offset (±1e-6) on all grids.

title: lbm: Han's wall-function bounce does not reproduce its own A20 channel (C_f +53 % MRT, −52 % HRR)
body:
### Current behaviour

Han, Ooka & Kikumoto's on-node wall-function bounce (Fluid Dyn. Res. 53:045506, 2021, eq. 14), `spalding_bounce` on plane walls, is on develop. Its own reproduction case fails (docs/verification.md, "Wall-modelled LES: Han, Ooka & Kikumoto not reproduced at A20"). The A20 channel (Re_τ 640) was run with a gate fixed beforehand: ε_u⁺ and the log-law intercept b within 15 % of the paper's Tables 2 and 3.

| Collision, SGS | U_b⁺ | C_f vs Dean | ε (paper 0.057) | b (paper 6.4) |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| MRT, Smagorinsky C_s 0.1, Van Driest (the paper's) | 14.44 | +53 % | 0.248 | 1.92 |
| HRR σ 0.99, Vreman C_s 0.18 | 28.77 | −54 % | 0.535 | 15.23 |
| HRR σ 0.99, Smagorinsky C_s 0.1, Van Driest | 27.94 | −52 % | 0.491 | 14.30 |
| HRR, dynamic σ, Vreman C_s 0.18 | 28.94 | −55 % | 0.607 | 9.04 |

The recorded explanation is energy pile-up for MRT (the documented under-resolved MRT failure, Nathen et al. 2018) and about half the right drag for HRR. Neither has been traced to a cause. The Han extension to obstacles (#1046–#1048) is on hold until this plane-wall case reproduces, since it builds on this wall.

### Expected behaviour

The A20 channel reproduces the paper within the pre-set 15 % gate on the paper's own collision and SGS settings. Failing that, a root cause is found and stated: our implementation of eq. 14 (or its forcing, sampling height, or wall-distance convention), the collision, the SGS model, or a set-up difference from the paper.

### Notes

- Recorded on an NVIDIA GB10 GPU in f32, before the libm (#1043) and #1015 changes. Re-measure on current develop first.
- Paper: arXiv 2009.04352 (read).

title: lbm-gpu: one-signed f32 momentum drift in TRT, and check_les's underived 1e-4 bar
body:
### Current behaviour

Found while diagnosing #1007's `sa::the_sa_channel_follows_the_cpu` (expert notes: swarm board `lbm-dd/expert-1007.md`), measured on an Apple M4 Max (Metal):

- **Regularized and HRR collisions on the GPU.** Their velocity drifted from the CPU by a one-signed f32 rounding of momentum: linear at about 0.88·2⁻²⁴ of the peak per step, 1.05e-4 after 2000 steps. #1015 (af8214f1) fixes it; on develop the same case is at 8.8e-7.
- **TRT on the GPU** has the same one-signed drift at about a fifth of the rate: 2.07e-5 after 2000 steps and 7.48e-5 after 8000, without SA. #1015's projection doesn't cover TRT.
- **`check_les`'s 1e-4 velocity bar** (lbm-gpu verification) is not derived. The tightest worst-case bound, N·u with u = 2⁻²⁴, is 1.19e-4 at N = 2000, so the bar sits just below the round-off it's meant to allow.

### Expected behaviour

- **TRT:** decide whether TRT gets the same mass and momentum projection as #1015 (checked against Guo forcing).
- **Bar:** derive `check_les`'s bar from f32 round-off, the case's step count and the collision. If a derived bar would also pass an unprojected drift, test the projection directly instead, as #1015's single-step test does.

title: lbm: Poiseuille mid-channel error converges at order 1.45 with a pressure outlet
body:
### Current behaviour

Measured while finishing #1005 (MRT velocity inlet), Apple M4 Max, `crates/lbm/tests/mrt_inlet.rs` heavy Poiseuille case:

- Next to the inlet, the velocity error against the exact parabola is 1.15e-3 at h = 16 and 2.87e-4 at h = 32: order 2.01.
- Mid-channel, it is 5.3e-3 and 1.9e-3: order 1.45.

The inlet itself is second order. The suspicion is that the pressure outlet's error reaches back into the channel. That hasn't been isolated.

### Expected behaviour

Second order throughout a Poiseuille channel with a velocity inlet and a pressure outlet. If the outlet condition's published order is lower, the manual should say so and the test should check that order.

### What's needed

1. Measure the order with the outlet replaced by a periodic or exact-velocity boundary, to isolate the outlet's share.
2. Check the outlet's treatment against the paper it cites.
3. Assert the order the paper supports.

title: Grid Static: a linear static solve on a background grid (finite cell method), for parts and assemblies
body: ### Current behaviour Every static solve in FieldCraft needs a volume mesh of the part. That is the right tool for a model built for analysis, but it is the slow part of a design check, and some geometry does not mesh well at all: - **Imported surface meshes** (STL, 3MF from a CAD system) keep every triangle of the file as a face of the tet mesh, so the mesh is as fine as the file, however coarse a mesh was asked for. - **Thin-walled parts** (sheet metal, tubes) need quadratic tetrahedra to bend correctly, and the sheet's thickness and its bends set their size, not the size asked for. The sheet-metal tray of `crates/fcm/tests/tray.rs` (2 mm steel, 400 × 300 mm, four bent walls, holes and open corners) gives about 156,000 quadratic tetrahedra whatever size is asked, from 25 down to 4 mm. Its solve has 918,000 unknowns and is refused unless `max_factor_entries` is raised to 1.5 billion; meshing and solving take about 66 s on `develop` (44 s to mesh, 22 s to solve). - **Assemblies** need every body meshed and every contact face tied by hand. ### What you need and why A mechanical engineer checking a design wants stress and deflection of the part or the assembly as it comes from CAD, on the first click: no meshing, no ties, no element choices. The answer should say how far it can be trusted, and the settings that matter should be few and plain. Because it asks for so little (no mesh, no element choices, four settings), this would also be an excellent addition to SolidCraft, as a quick stress check right where the part is designed. The solver crate would not need to change for that: it takes a body as triangles with a tag for each face, plus supports and loads on those faces, and it does not depend on SolidCraft. ### Expected behaviour A command `solve.static.grid` (**Solve ▸ Grid Static**) that solves a linear static step of a body, or of every body of the design or of the imported surfaces, with no volume mesh: - The body is set in a grid of cubic cells with high-order shape functions; the surface only cuts the cells (the finite cell method). Cells are divided where the surface curves tightly and, in rounds, where the solution is least resolved. - Bodies that touch are bonded (or slide) where they touch, found automatically and kept as connections in the model that the user can change. - The step's supports and loads apply as they are, on the geometry's faces. Results are read on the surface: contours, probe, reactions, and a warning when the result is still changing or the peak sits at a notch that has no converged value. - Large models are solved by iteration (conjugate gradients with a two-level preconditioner), smaller ones by the existing sparse factorization. - The form shows four settings (step, body, cell size, adaptive rounds) and folds the rest under **Advanced settings**. I have a working implementation on a fork (`eaglechlapf/fieldcraft`, branch `grid-static`, rebased on today's `develop`): a new crate `crates/fcm` at layer 2, the command, its form and docs (`docs/grid-static.md`), with tests against closed-form and published values. Would you like it as one pull request, or split (the sparse-factorization speed-ups in `crates/solver` first, then the grid solver)? ### Pictures All four on FieldCraft's sample **File ▸ Samples ▸ Bracket Without a Mesh** (the filleted steel bracket clamped under its foot, 2 kN on its top). 1. **Solve ▸ Grid Static:** the form as it opens, four settings, all automatic. 2. The same form with **Advanced settings** opened. 3. A setting's help, with a picture drawn in the theme's colours. 4. The result after OK, with no mesh made: von Mises stress, 212.5 MPa on the fillet, where the oracle case `tests/oracle/filleted-bracket-fillet-stress` gives 213 MPa. ### References - J. Parvizian, A. Düster, E. Rank, *Finite cell method: h- and p-extension for embedded domain problems in solid mechanics*, Comput. Mech. 41(1):121–133, 2007. - A. Düster, J. Parvizian, Z. Yang, E. Rank, *The finite cell method for three-dimensional problems of solid mechanics*, Comput. Methods Appl. Mech. Engrg. 197:3768–3782, 2008. - N. Zander, T. Bog, S. Kollmannsberger, D. Schillinger, E. Rank, *Multi-level hp-adaptivity: high-order mesh adaptivity without the difficulties of constraining hanging nodes*, Comput. Mech. 55(3):499–517, 2015. - B. Szabó, I. Babuška, *Finite Element Analysis*, Wiley 1991 (hierarchic shape functions and the refinement indicator). - W. Dörfler, *A convergent adaptive algorithm for Poisson's equation*, SIAM J. Numer. Anal. 33(3):1106–1124, 1996. - A. Hansbo, P. Hansbo, *An unfitted finite element method, based on Nitsche's method, for elliptic interface problems*, Comput. Methods Appl. Mech. Engrg. 191:5537–5552, 2002; C. Annavarapu, M. Hautefeuille, J. E. Dolbow, *A robust Nitsche's formulation for interface problems*, Comput. Methods Appl. Mech. Engrg. 225–228:44–54, 2012 (bonded and sliding bodies). - A. Toselli, O. Widlund, *Domain Decomposition Methods: Algorithms and Theory*, Springer 2005 (the iteration's preconditioner); M. Arioli, *A stopping criterion for the conjugate gradient algorithm in a finite element method framework*, Numer. Math. 97:1–24, 2004. - Verification: the Kirsch plate with a hole, NAFEMS LE1, patch tests, and FieldCraft's own oracle case `tests/oracle/filleted-bracket-fillet-stress`.

title: Restore Intel macOS packages for regular releases
body:
### Current behavior

PR #942 dropped Intel macOS packages in 0.8.0 after the universal package took 107 minutes to build from a cold cache. The Apple silicon package is the macOS download for current releases.

### What I need and why

Could FieldCraft ship an Intel macOS release package again, starting with the next release? I still use an Intel Mac for FieldCraft. Keeping older Macs useful is something I value about the Craft app community.

### Expected behavior

Would a separate native `macos-15-intel` packaging job be acceptable for regular releases? It could run alongside the Apple silicon job with its own Rust cache and use the existing packaging script to produce an `x86_64` DMG and CLI ZIP. The release could sign and publish both architectures through the same pipeline. The nightly schedule could keep its current selection of packages.

I can prepare a focused PR with the workflow, architecture-specific update selection, and release notes if this approach fits the release process.

### References

- #942 explains why Intel packaging was removed.
- [Native Intel packaging run on my fork](https://github.com/JohannesMaierhofer/fieldcraft/actions/runs/45054540735). The packaging step built and checked the Intel app and CLI in about 38 minutes. This validation run used the STEP-import branch, ad hoc signing, and a faster test build profile with LTO disabled.

title: fracture: model.crack.create and the domain-integral J (RFC 0002 port steps 2–3)
body:
### Current behaviour

FieldCraft has no crack definition and no fracture parameters. RFC 0002 (docs/rfc/0002-warp3d-fracture.md) decided how they come: FieldCraft ports WARP3D's fracture capabilities to Rust and does not run WARP3D beside it (§6.1). Steps 2 and 3 of its port order (§5) need no WARP3D code at all: both are written from the published papers.

### Expected behaviour

**Step 2: `model.crack.create`** (RFC 0002 §6.2), a model definition, not a parameter of one command:
- the front as a node set, ordered or not, chained into an open path or a closed loop, taking hex20 mid-side nodes along (hex and collapsed-wedge fronts; tet fronts refused with a clear message);
- the crack-plane normal, given or inferred from the symmetry conditions on the front;
- `symmetric` for a half model;
- the number of rings of integration domains;
- the weighting along the front: `pointwise` (tent functions inside, ramps at open ends) or `front_average`.

**Step 3: the domain-integral J on linear-elastic solids**, from C. F. Shih, B. Moran, T. Nakamura, *Energy release rate along a three-dimensional crack front in a thermally stressed body*, Int. J. Fracture 30:79–102, 1986, and B. Moran, C. F. Shih, *A general treatment of crack tip contour integrals*, Int. J. Fracture 35:295–310, 1987. J per station and per ring in the session's results, `solve.probe` reads them, and K_I from J under plane strain.

**Verification** (docs/verification.md), on our own models built in SolidCraft from the published descriptions:
- the semi-elliptical surface crack in a finite plate against I. S. Raju, J. C. Newman, Eng. Fract. Mech. 11(4):817–829, 1979, and X. Wang, R. Bell, Eng. Fract. Mech. 71(9):1477–1496, 2004;
- CT and SENB specimens against their handbook K solutions;
- ring-to-ring path independence of the outer rings as a mesh invariant.

WARP3D's verification inputs (`verification/test87` and the like) are not copied, and WARP3D's outputs are not references (RFC 0002 §6.3).

### For @ExMonsterJoker

We've read your two reports on `warp3d/wedge6-export` (the test_87 integration and the API TR 579-A study). They're careful work, and the export round-trips WARP3D faithfully. The sidecar route itself (`backend: "warp3d"`, the runner, the result reader) is the one RFC 0002 §6.1 decided against, so it won't land. Much of it carries straight into this issue, though, and you'd be the natural person to take it:
- your crack-front ordering, normal and symmetry resolution, ring ranges and `pointwise` weighting are step 2;
- your crack-tube finding (r_box below the front's curvature radius a²/c: free-surface ring spread from 11 % to 0.23 %) belongs in the meshing notes;
- Raju–Newman, Wang & Bell and API TR 579-A are exactly the references we want, here solved by FieldCraft's own J.

Things in the reports to fix wherever this goes:
- **Units.** test_87 is kip/inch/ksi, but the procedure picks `in-lbf-s-psi`. Force and stress are then stored 1000× off in SI; it only matches because the error cancels on the way out.
- **β.** β at 90° (0.0914 against TR 579-A's 0.0541) is a 69 % miss, not "low-β regime captured".
- **The material curve.** The 0.58 σ_YS table onset and the ε_p0 shift change the material relative to the reference curve, and need a cited source.
- **Circular comparisons.** "FieldCraft vs Manual WARP3D" checks the export, not the physics. TR 579-A's tables come from WARP3D, so matching them with WARP3D is circular.

If you want it, comment `/claim` here. Whether to keep a WARP3D deck export for people who run WARP3D themselves (RFC 0002 §6.4) is still open; that's separate from this issue.

### References

- RFC 0002, §5, §6.2, §6.3.
- The papers above.

title: solver: faer as an opt-in factorization backend behind Factor
body:
### Current behaviour

`fieldcraft-solver` factors with its own supernodal left-looking Cholesky and LDLᵀ, multithreaded with a fixed operation order, so the CPU result is bit-for-bit the same on every machine and thread count. docs/adr/0001-libraries.md (2026-10-13) turned `faer` (MIT) down as the default for that reason: it selects SIMD kernels by CPU feature at run time (AVX2, AVX-512, NEON), which changes floating-point reduction order between machines, and it is a large dependency tree for the browser build. The ADR names the remedy if speed on large models matters: `faer` behind the same `Factor` interface, with a stated tolerance instead of bit-identity, as the GPU exception already does.

### What you need and why

`faer` is reported to factor about 2× faster on large models. Large structural models (and the complex systems RFC 0001 brings) are where factorization time dominates.

### Expected behaviour

- `faer` behind `Factor` as an opt-in backend; our factor stays the default and the reference.
- Not built for `wasm32` (feature-gated off), so the browser build is unchanged.
- Results checked against our factor within a stated relative tolerance on the solver's tests and the oracle cases; that tolerance and the opt-in are documented the way the GPU exception is (AGENTS.md "Determinism").
- Measured speed-up on our own large models (crank arm, a few hundred thousand to a few million equations), at 1 and N threads, before and after; the ADR updated with the numbers and the decision.
- Real and, once the scalar-generic factor lands (RFC 0001 phase 1, #881), complex-symmetric.

### Open for the maintainer

- Where the opt-in lives (a solver setting on the step, a session setting, or an environment-free CLI flag; AGENTS.md rules out environment switches in library code).
- Whether the oracle runs on both backends in CI.

### References

- docs/adr/0001-libraries.md, "Linear algebra: our own".
- RFC 0001, docs/rfc/0001-electromagnetics.md §3.2 and §8.3.

title: Explicit self contact: a layer squeezed through its thickness touches itself (false contact force), with a fix and self-contact verification
body:
### What I am trying to do

Crush soft parts in an `explicit_dynamic` step with general contact on all exterior faces: a
foam pad pressed in a die, a rubber tube flattened between two punches, a lattice whose struts
fold onto each other. General contact already does self contact (single-surface contact, every
face against every other one that shares no node with it), and a body that folds onto itself
does stop at itself. But a body that is only squeezed through its thickness, with nothing
touching, gets contact forces between its own faces:

- a foam layer one hex8 thick, squeezed by 60 % in a closed die, with `interaction.contact.general`
  on all faces: peak contact force 193 N where there should be none, and the motion differs from
  the same run without contact;
- the same layer two elements thick squeezed by 80 %: 1 216 N.

The cause is in `crates/explicit/src/contact.rs`: a point counts as in contact when it is behind a
facing main face by less than half the main face's element is thick, and that thickness is the
undeformed one. The top and bottom faces of a hex face each other and share no node, so once the
layer is squeezed below half its thickness (below 1/(2n) for n layers), its far side reads as a
penetration.

I found no issue or PR on self contact in explicit dynamics (#88, closed, delivered it; #182 is
about implicit self contact for the bellows example).

### Proposal

Two rules in the explicit contact search, nothing in the model or the commands:

1. A face never meets a face of its own element (as the initial-penetration check already does
   with `owner`).
2. The depth limit is half the smaller of the main face's element's undeformed and current
   thickness (current volume over current face area, the trilinear hex volume by the 2 × 2 × 2
   rule, exact). The far side of a squeezed layer is always at least about one current element
   away, so it is never taken for a surface the near side has passed; a real penetration is p/ε,
   which does not grow when the element is squeezed.

Where no element is squeezed below half its thickness, nothing changes: the depths and therefore
the accepted integration points are the same, and the existing contact tests give the same
results bit for bit (checked with result digests before and after on four models).

### I have it working, if you want it as a PR

On a local branch off `develop` (a6d29ed5), about 60 lines in `contact.rs` plus a new test file,
`crates/explicit/tests/self_contact.rs`, and the manual:

- **One body against two:** two bars joined by a soft hinge cell over their joint (one body,
  general contact on all its faces) collide like the same bars unjoined with a contact pair: peak
  force −0.022 %, contact time 0.000 %, rebound velocities within 1.6·10⁻³ v₀; both within 1.2 %
  of wave theory's contact time 2L/c and 0.3 % of its force ρcAv₀/2.
- **Momentum and energy in a self-impact:** a U-shaped body whose arms are thrown at each other
  keeps its linear momentum to 5·10⁻¹⁵; its angular momentum to 1.6·10⁻⁸ frictionless; with
  μ = 0.3 it changes by 8.5·10⁻⁷ against the bound δ_max μ ∫F_n dt = 1.7·10⁻⁵ that the friction
  couple allows (friction acts at a node and, reversed, at the face point under it, an arm of the
  penetration); balance 1.6·10⁻⁴; bit for bit on one and four threads.
- **A ring crushed flat:** half a neo-Hookean ring in plane strain, crushed by two punches until
  its walls meet. Without contact the walls pass through each other by 27 % of the wall; with
  general contact (on the inner surface, or on all faces) they stop within 0.0087 (8.7 % of the
  wall) and the contact carries 99.6 % (98 %) of the punch's force, 18 times what bending alone
  takes. The force at the last increment, 7.69, lies inside the penalty law's bracket
  ε W ∫ d dx = 7.1 to 11.1 from the measured overlap (ε = γ min(m/A)/Δt² with the stable
  increments of the last samples, which swing by 20 % there).
- **No false contact:** a cantilever flung to a tip deflection of 0.78 of its length, a thick
  tube with a small bore ovalising, and the two squeezed layers above give the same frames bit
  for bit as without contact, with no contact force.
- **Cost** (a heavy test, a slab tumbling freely): 13, 13, 6.4 and 5.1 µs per exterior face and
  increment for 192 to 8 704 faces, in a debug build on a shared machine, so linear in the faces.
- The search is still rebuilt from the positions every increment and keeps no state, so a
  checkpoint needs nothing new for it (the friction forces and the cached mass per area stay the
  only contact state).
- `cargo fmt`, `cargo clippy -D warnings` and the tests of `fieldcraft-explicit` pass;
  `docs/features.md` is unchanged (no command changed).

### Questions before I open a PR

1. **The depth rule.** Half the smaller of the undeformed and current thickness keeps results the
   same where nothing is squeezed, but under a very high pressure on an element crushed below
   half its thickness, points deeper than p/ε > h/2 now let go a little sooner. Is that the
   trade you want, or would you rather keep the undeformed limit and only add the own-element
   rule (which fixes the one-layer case but not two layers squeezed by more than 75 %)?
2. **An oracle case.** The ring crush or the hinged bars could become an oracle case
   (`explicit-self-contact-*`). Wanted in this PR?
3. **Scope.** Not in this slice: edge-to-edge contact, eroding contact (faces exposed by eroded
   elements joining the surface), a penalty per face pair instead of one per contact (general
   contact on a model of very different parts takes its lightest part's penalty). Which of these
   would you take next?

I can `/claim` this and open the draft PR once you say which way to go on 1.

title: Stress-life (S-N) fatigue of a linear static result: rainflow, mean-stress corrections, Miner damage
body:
### What I am trying to do

I have a linear static result for a bracket under a reference load, and the load really comes and
goes: a cycle from zero to full, or a measured history of the load. I want to know where the part
cracks first and after how many cycles, or how much of its life one block of the history uses.
Today the answer is a hand calculation from a probed stress, one node at a time.

ROADMAP M20 lists "fatigue (S–N and ε–N with mean-stress corrections, rainflow counting, Paris
crack growth)" as planned. I found no issue or pull request for it, so this is one, for the S-N
part only.

### Proposal

Post-processing of a solved linear static step, nothing new in a solver:

1. S-N data on the material, an optional block:

```json
{"command": "model.material.fatigue", "params": {"name": "Steel", "fatigue": {
  "curve": {"type": "basquin", "coefficient": 1000, "exponent": -0.1},
  "endurance_limit": 150, "ultimate_strength": 800, "yield_strength": 600}}}
```

   Basquin in reversals, σa = σf′ (2N)^b (the cycle form S = A N^b has A = σf′ 2^b), or a table
   interpolated on log-log axes; an optional endurance limit (infinite life at and below it).

2. How the step's load repeats, one assessment per step:

```json
{"command": "model.fatigue.set", "params": {"step": "Load",
  "loading": {"type": "history", "factors": [0, 1, -0.4, 0.8, -1, 0]},
  "measure": "signed_von_mises", "mean_stress": "goodman", "stress_factor": 1}}
```

   `constant_amplitude` (max and min load factors), `stress_ratio` (R), or `history` (rainflow by
   ASTM E1049-85 §5.4.4 for a history that happens once, or Downing & Socie 1982 algorithm I for a
   repeating block). Measures: von Mises signed by the largest principal stress, or the largest
   principal stress itself. Mean stress: none, Goodman, Gerber, Soderberg (no benefit taken from a
   compressive mean). Palmgren–Miner damage. One `stress_factor` multiplies the amplitudes (a K_f
   the mesh does not hold, or 1/k for a surface or size factor).

3. Results as three new contour fields, `fatigue_log_life`, `fatigue_damage` and
   `fatigue_safety_factor`, which `results.contour`, `solve.probe` and `results.path` show, and a
   summary command `results.fatigue` (the counted cycles, the node of least life with its
   coordinates, governing amplitude and mean, the least safety factor, counts of nodes with
   infinite life, static failures, yield at the peak load and reads beyond a table, warnings).

The proportional-loading assumption is the method's: every stress component follows one factor.
Proportional loading is the only thing the input can express, so nothing non-proportional reaches
the method; nodes above yield at the peak load are counted and warned about.

### I have a first slice working, if you want it as a PR

On a local branch off `develop` (a6d29ed5), about 2 400 lines with tests and docs:

- Model: `Material.fatigue` (`Fatigue`, `SnCurve`, `SnPoint`) and `Model.fatigue` (assessments
  by step name, renamed with the step and removed with it). Both optional and absent by default.
- Neither is a step input: `Model::step_inputs` serializes the materials without their fatigue
  data, so adding or editing the data or the loading keeps the step's result current, and a
  material without the block hashes exactly as before (saved results stay current).
- Nothing new in the results encoding (`MCRSLT05` unchanged): the fields are computed from the
  saved result and the saved definitions whenever they are shown, so they survive save and open.
- Method in `fieldcraft_fem::fatigue`, the fields in `fieldcraft_engine::fatigue`, commands with
  forms (units convert through the forms), catalogue entries and a manual page
  (`docs/manual/structural/fatigue.md`, with a limitations section).
- Verification, all against theory or hand calculation:
  - Basquin read both ways from N = 1 to 10⁹: exact to 10⁻¹²; log-log table exact at its points and
    at geometric means;
  - Goodman, Gerber and Soderberg equivalent amplitudes and safety factors against their formulas
    (hand values: σ_ar 200, 160, 225; n 4/3 and 1.2; Gerber's point on its parabola), to 10⁻¹³;
  - rainflow of the history −2, 1, −3, 5, −1, 3, −4, 4, −2 (the worked example usually given for
    ASTM E1049; I wrote it from memory and did not have the standard open, so the reference here is my
    own hand count by the standard's procedure): ½ × 3, 1½ × 4, ½ × 6, 1 × 8, ½ × 9, with every mean; as
    a repeating block, full cycles of 3, 4, 7 and 9;
  - a uniform hex8 bar at 200 MPa: every node's life is Basquin's at the formula's equivalent
    amplitude to 10⁻⁹ in log₁₀ N, for R = −1 and R = 0 under each correction; endurance limit,
    infinite life and safety factor 0.75 and 1.5 exact;
  - a two-block history (3 cycles at ±1, 5 at ±0.5) on the bar: Miner's 3/N₁ + 5/N₂ to 10⁻⁹;
  - the plate with a hole of the `kirsch-plate-plane-stress` oracle case at S = 100 MPa fully
    reversed: the least life is at the top of the hole, Kt = 3.0029, N = 83 867 against 84 675 from
    Kt = 3 (−0.95 %, log₁₀ N off by 0.004, inside the 0.086 the oracle case's 2 % Kt band allows);
  - save and open give the same fields bit for bit; hostile curves, strengths, ratios, factors,
    histories (over 100 000 factors), names and choices are refused and change nothing.
- `cargo fmt`, `cargo clippy -D warnings` and the tests of the crates touched (model, fem, engine)
  pass; `docs/features.md` regenerated. No new dependency, nothing native-only.

### Questions before I open a PR

1. **File format.** `Material` and `Model` deny unknown fields, so an older FieldCraft refuses a
   file with either new block. Stay in `fieldcraft/3` as an optional addition, as the format page
   allows, or step to format 4?
2. **Where the loading lives.** I keyed assessments by step name (one per step) so the fields can
   find theirs without a new field in the results view. Would you rather have named assessments
   (several per step) and a way to pick one for the contour?
3. **Life on a log scale.** The life field is log₁₀ of cycles (blocks of a history), infinite below
   the endurance limit and drawn in the top band. Is that the field you want, or the plain life
   with a log legend in the renderer?
4. **The app.** The desktop contour menu lists fields from `Field::available(result)`, which has no
   model, so the fatigue fields are reachable only through the command; a linear static animation
   would scale them like stresses. I left `ui-egui` alone. Want those two in the same PR or after?
5. **Scope.** Not in this slice: strain-life (ε-N, Morrow, SWT) and notch plasticity, multiaxial
   (critical plane), several load cases with their own histories, temperature- or
   finish-dependent curves, welds, an oracle case, VTU export of the fatigue fields, and any
   shipped material data (none without a citation). Which of these do you want before it can
   merge?

I can `/claim` this and open the draft PR once you say which way to go on 1 and 2.

title: Viscoelastic hyperelastic material (Prony series) in explicit dynamics, so a rubber impact loses energy
body:
### What I am trying to do

Simulate the drop and rebound of a printed elastomer part (a thermoplastic elastomer lattice,
neo-Hookean in the model) with an `explicit_dynamic` step, an initial velocity and a rigid wall.
The run works today, but every material FieldCraft has for it is perfectly elastic, so the part
bounces back with all of its energy apart from what ends up as vibration. The elastomer's own
loss (its rebound resilience is 60 to 80 %) is the number I need, and there is no material that
has one.

ROADMAP M17 lists "finite-strain viscoelasticity (Prony series)" as planned. I found no issue
for it, so this is one.

### Proposal

An optional `viscoelastic` block on a material that has a `hyperelastic` block:

```json
{"name": "TPE", "elastic": {"type": "isotropic", "young": 30, "poisson": 0.45}, "density": 1.0e-9,
 "hyperelastic": {"type": "neo_hookean"},
 "viscoelastic": {"terms": [{"g": 0.3, "tau": 0.001}, {"g": 0.1, "tau": 0.05}]}}
```

- Shear relaxation G(t)/G₀ = g∞ + Σ gᵢ exp(−t/τᵢ), g∞ = 1 − Σ gᵢ > 0. The volume response stays
  elastic.
- The elastic and hyperelastic constants are the **instantaneous** response. That keeps the
  explicit stable increment as it is today (no relaxed state is stiffer).
- Model: Simo 1987 (CMAME 60:153–173; Simo & Hughes 1998, §10.3; Holzapfel 2000, §6.10), with
  the history as material tensors, so it is objective, the Kirchhoff stress stays deviatoric and
  the pressure (the tetrahedra's averaged nodal pressure included) stays with U(J). Time
  integration by the recurrence of Taylor, Pister & Goudreau 1970.

### I have a first slice working, if you want it as a PR

On a local branch off `develop` (a6d29ed5), about 700 lines with tests and docs:

- `fieldcraft_fem::viscoelastic::Prony` (the material-point update), `Material.viscoelastic` in
  the model with validation and unit conversion, the form field and the `model.material.create`
  text, per-element history in `fieldcraft-explicit`, hex8 and tet4.
- A nonlinear static step, which has no time, takes the fully relaxed material (g∞ on the
  isochoric response). The linear procedures use the elastic constants alone, as they do for
  plasticity. The Abaqus, LS-DYNA and Nastran writers refuse a viscoelastic material.
- Verification, all against theory:
  - a held strain relaxes exactly as the series (round-off);
  - storage modulus, loss modulus and the loss per cycle in small harmonic shear against the
    generalized Maxwell closed forms (Christensen 1982, §1.6), within 10⁻⁵;
  - objectivity under a superposed rotation; the fast and slow loading limits;
  - explicit hex8 and tet4 blocks pulled in uniaxial strain at three rates against the material
    point integrated along the same path (five digits);
  - a block set vibrating keeps its motion when elastic and loses it when viscoelastic, with the
    energy balance closed;
  - the static step against the neo-Hookean closed form with the relaxed shear modulus.
- What it gives on the case I started from, in a small form: a 40 mm neo-Hookean ball (E = 30 MPa,
  ν = 0.45, 28,660 tet4) hitting a rigid wall at 5.94 m/s. Elastic: 98.0 % of the drop height
  comes back (the rest is vibration). One Prony term at the contact time (τ = 0.33 ms):
  g = 0.146 gives 84.1 %, g = 0.264 gives 72.7 %. Contact lasts 0.93 ms (Hertz estimate 1.05 ms),
  and the energy balance closes to 10⁻⁸ of the kinetic energy in all three.
- `cargo fmt`, `cargo clippy -D warnings` and the tests of the six crates touched (model, fem,
  explicit, solver, decks, engine) pass; `docs/features.md` is unchanged.
- No panics in non-test code; hostile series (empty, Σ g ≥ 1, zero or negative τ, NaN, more than
  32 terms, unknown keys) are refused by the model and the command.

### Questions before I open a PR

1. **File format.** `Material` denies unknown fields, so an older FieldCraft refuses a file with
   the new block. `docs/formats/fieldcraft.md` lets optional additions stay in the current
   format, but its note that no released FieldCraft reads format 3 is out of date (0.7.5 to
   0.8.1 do). Stay in `fieldcraft/3`, or format 4 with a step?
2. **Steps without time.** Is "nonlinear static takes the relaxed material, linear steps the
   elastic constants as given" what you want, or should these steps refuse a viscoelastic
   material until there is a step with a duration?
3. **Reporting the loss.** The element energy is the work of the stress, so the dissipation sits
   inside `internal` and the balance closes. A separate `viscoelastic` energy (as `plastic` is
   for plastic work) would mean a new field in `Energies` and a results-encoding bump
   (`MCRSLT05` to `06`). I left it out; say if you want it in the same PR.
4. **Scope.** Not in this slice: small-strain viscoelasticity for elastic materials, bulk
   relaxation, WLF or Arrhenius shift, a `model.material.viscoelastic` command of its own, deck
   output, an oracle case. Which of these do you want before it can merge?

I can `/claim` this and open the draft PR as soon as you say which way to go on 1 and 2.

title: Return the traced streamline points (results.streamlines) and export fluid results to a file
body:
### Current behaviour

For a solved fluid step, `results.streamlines` traces the lines (the reply says how many: `"traced": {"streamlines": 2, "points":
319, "seeds": 2, "no_start": 0}`) but the points themselves are only drawn in the viewport: the reply has no coordinates. And
`results.export.vtu` on the same step fails with `fluid results are per cell; not supported yet`. So a script, an MCP agent or another
program driving FieldCraft headless cannot get the streamlines or the flow field out, except point by point with `solve.probe`.

Script below: plane Poiseuille flow between two walls, parabolic inlet 10 mm/s, pressure outlet. It solves in
about a second.

```json
[
 {"command": "model.units", "params": {"system": "mm-t-s-N-MPa"}},
 {"command": "model.material.create", "params": {"name": "Oil", "density": 1e-9, "fluid": {"type": "newtonian", "viscosity": 1e-7}}},
 {"command": "model.fluid_domain.create", "params": {"name": "Flow", "material": "Oil", "min": [0, 0, 0], "max": [40, 10, 2], "spacing": 0.5, "faces": {"x_min": {"type": "velocity", "velocity": [10, 0, 0], "profile": "parabolic"}, "x_max": {"type": "pressure", "pressure": 0}, "z_min": {"type": "periodic"}, "z_max": {"type": "periodic"}}}},
 {"command": "model.step.create", "params": {"name": "Run", "procedure": {"type": "fluid", "domain": "Flow", "end_time": 2, "frames": 2}}},
 {"command": "solve.fluid", "params": {"step": "Run", "backend": "cpu"}},
 {"command": "results.streamlines", "params": {"step": "Run", "seeds": [[0.25, 5, 1], [0.25, 2.5, 1]], "max_steps": 200}},
 {"command": "results.animate", "params": {"on": true}},
 {"command": "results.export.vtu", "params": {"step": "Run", "path": "flow.vtu", "encoding": "ascii"}}
]
```
- `results.streamlines` reply: keys `contour, frames, ports, slice, stale, streamlines, surface, time, traced, view`; `traced` has the
  counts only.
- `results.export.vtu`: error `fluid results are per cell; not supported yet`.

### What you need and why

Driving FieldCraft headless (scripts, an MCP agent, or another program that shows the results itself), the streamlines and the flow field cannot be read back, except point by point with `solve.probe`.

### Expected behaviour

1. `results.streamlines` (or an option such as `"return_points": true`) replying with each line's points (and the speed at them),
   like `solve.probe` with `line` does for one line.
2. A file export of the fluid frames: VTK image data (`.vti`) or rectilinear grid with cell data (velocity, pressure, temperature),
   one file per saved frame plus a `.pvd`, so the flow can be post-processed in ParaView.

(For the record, the solution itself is right: pressure drop 3.182e-6 MPa against 8 μ u_max L / h² = 3.16e-6 between the
first and last cell layers (+0.7 %), inflow 133.50 mm³/s against 2/3 u_max h W = 133.33 (+0.13 %).)

### Version and platform

FieldCraft 0.8.1 (`fieldcraft-cli` from the Windows x64 release package, `mcp --headless`, CPU); Windows 11 Pro x64

---
*Found while integrating FieldCraft as the solver of a CAD program; every number was checked against the closed-form solution given above.*

title: Distributing coupling: equal nodal weights make a uniformly pulled end face over-compliant (hex20)
body:
### Observed failure

A bar in pure tension, pulled through a reference point with a **distributing** coupling to its end face, should behave like the
same bar under a uniform traction on that face (Saint-Venant: the coupling should only matter close to the face, and for a
uniform state not at all, since the equivalent nodal loads of a uniform traction on hex20 faces are the consistent ones). With
the coupling the end face does not stay uniform: the reference point moves 3.5 % more than F L/(E A), the end face warps and the
von Mises stress at its corners reaches 43 MPa instead of 10 MPa. The manual already mentions that the distributing coupling uses
equal weights per node (`pure-bending-coupling`, known failure); this is the same cause in the simplest possible case.

### Reproduction

Script below: steel bar 100 × 10 × 10 mm, hex20 20 × 2 × 2, three symmetry planes, two static steps:
`Coupled` (1000 N on the reference point, distributing coupling on translations) and `Pressure` (−10 MPa pressure on the same face,
the same resultant).

```json
[
 {"command": "model.units", "params": {"system": "mm-t-s-N-MPa"}},
 {"command": "mesh.block", "params": {"body": "Bar", "kind": "hex20", "corners": [[0,0,0],[100,0,0],[100,10,0],[0,10,0],[0,0,10],[100,0,10],[100,10,10],[0,10,10]], "divisions": [20,2,2], "faces": {"6": "x0", "4": "x1", "3": "y0", "1": "z0"}}},
 {"command": "model.set.create", "params": {"name": "all", "geometry": [{"body": "Bar"}]}},
 {"command": "model.set.create", "params": {"name": "x0", "geometry": [{"body": "Bar", "face": "x0"}]}},
 {"command": "model.set.create", "params": {"name": "x1", "geometry": [{"body": "Bar", "face": "x1"}]}},
 {"command": "model.set.create", "params": {"name": "y0", "geometry": [{"body": "Bar", "face": "y0"}]}},
 {"command": "model.set.create", "params": {"name": "z0", "geometry": [{"body": "Bar", "face": "z0"}]}},
 {"command": "model.material.create", "params": {"name": "Steel", "elastic": {"type": "isotropic", "young": 210000, "poisson": 0.3}}},
 {"command": "model.section.create", "params": {"name": "solid", "set": "all", "material": "Steel", "kind": {"type": "solid"}}},
 {"command": "model.boundary_condition.create", "params": {"name": "symx", "type": "symmetry", "target": {"set": "x0"}, "plane": "x"}},
 {"command": "model.boundary_condition.create", "params": {"name": "symy", "type": "symmetry", "target": {"set": "y0"}, "plane": "y"}},
 {"command": "model.boundary_condition.create", "params": {"name": "symz", "type": "symmetry", "target": {"set": "z0"}, "plane": "z"}},
 {"command": "model.reference_point.create", "params": {"name": "RP", "xyz": [100, 5, 5]}},
 {"command": "model.coupling.create", "params": {"name": "end", "reference_point": "RP", "set": "x1", "kind": "distributing", "dofs": [1, 2, 3]}},
 {"command": "model.load.create", "params": {"name": "pull_rp", "type": "force", "target": {"reference_point": "RP"}, "vector": [1000, 0, 0]}},
 {"command": "model.load.create", "params": {"name": "pull_p", "type": "pressure", "set": "x1", "magnitude": -10}},
 {"command": "model.step.create", "params": {"name": "Coupled", "procedure": {"type": "static"}, "boundary_conditions": ["symx", "symy", "symz"], "loads": ["pull_rp"]}},
 {"command": "model.step.create", "params": {"name": "Pressure", "procedure": {"type": "static"}, "boundary_conditions": ["symx", "symy", "symz"], "loads": ["pull_p"]}},
 {"command": "solve.static", "params": {"step": "Coupled"}},
 {"command": "solve.probe", "params": {"step": "Coupled", "at": [[100, 0, 0], [100, 5, 5], [100, 10, 10], [100, 0, 5], [50, 5, 5]]}},
 {"command": "solve.static", "params": {"step": "Pressure"}},
 {"command": "solve.probe", "params": {"step": "Pressure", "at": [[100, 0, 0], [100, 5, 5], [100, 10, 10], [100, 0, 5], [50, 5, 5]]}}
]
```

### Evidence

| | reference point u_x | end face u_x (corner, centre, edge mid) | max von Mises |
|---|---|---|---|
| `Pressure` | — (0.0047619) | 0.004762, 0.004762, 0.004762 | 10.000 MPa |
| `Coupled` (distributing) | **0.0049292 (+3.5 %)** | 0.005134 / 0.005410, 0.004707, 0.004858 | **42.99 MPa** |

At mid-length both steps give the same u_x = 0.002381 and 10 MPa, so the error is local to the coupled face but it changes the
reference point's motion, which is what users read as the "remote displacement".

### Expected behaviour

u_x = F L / (E A) = 1000 · 100 / (210000 · 100) = **0.0047619 mm**, uniform on the end face; σ_xx = 10 MPa everywhere.

### Investigation

Weight the distributing coupling with the face's consistent nodal weights (the same area weights `force` with `distribution: total`
uses), at least as an option (`"weighting": "area"`), like Abaqus' `*DISTRIBUTING` weighting methods.

### Version and platform

FieldCraft 0.8.1 (`fieldcraft-cli` from the Windows x64 release package, `mcp --headless`, CPU); Windows 11 Pro x64

---

title: Coupled temperature–displacement: a linear temperature field in a free bar gives spurious stresses and a warped end face
body:
### Observed failure

A free bar (three symmetry planes only) with a temperature of 20 °C held on one end and 120 °C on the other is solved with a
`coupled_temperature_displacement` step. The steady temperature field is exactly linear (checked: T = 70 °C at mid-length), so the
exact thermoelastic solution is stress-free with u_x = α ∫₀ˣ (T − T_ref) dx, uniform over every cross-section. FieldCraft returns the
right temperatures but a warped end face, a mid-length displacement 0.67 % too large, and up to 29 MPa of von Mises stress at nodes of
the end faces. The same happens with hex8 and a coarser mesh. A **uniform** temperature (both ends at 120 °C) is reproduced exactly.

### Reproduction

Run the script below, e.g. through `fieldcraft-cli` MCP `execute`, one command at a time, or
`fieldcraft-cli run 01-script.json`. It needs no geometry file (`mesh.block`).

```json
[
 {"command": "model.units", "params": {"system": "mm-t-s-N-MPa"}},
 {"command": "mesh.block", "params": {"body": "Bar", "kind": "hex20", "corners": [[0,0,0],[200,0,0],[200,20,0],[0,20,0],[0,0,20],[200,0,20],[200,20,20],[0,20,20]], "divisions": [40,4,4], "faces": {"6": "x0", "4": "x1", "3": "y0", "1": "z0"}}},
 {"command": "model.set.create", "params": {"name": "all", "geometry": [{"body": "Bar"}]}},
 {"command": "model.set.create", "params": {"name": "x0", "geometry": [{"body": "Bar", "face": "x0"}]}},
 {"command": "model.set.create", "params": {"name": "x1", "geometry": [{"body": "Bar", "face": "x1"}]}},
 {"command": "model.set.create", "params": {"name": "y0", "geometry": [{"body": "Bar", "face": "y0"}]}},
 {"command": "model.set.create", "params": {"name": "z0", "geometry": [{"body": "Bar", "face": "z0"}]}},
 {"command": "model.material.create", "params": {"name": "Steel", "elastic": {"type": "isotropic", "young": 210000, "poisson": 0.3}, "thermal": {"conductivity": 50, "expansion": 1.2e-5, "reference_temperature": 20}}},
 {"command": "model.section.create", "params": {"name": "solid", "set": "all", "material": "Steel", "kind": {"type": "solid"}}},
 {"command": "model.boundary_condition.create", "params": {"name": "Tcold", "type": "temperature", "target": {"set": "x0"}, "value": 20}},
 {"command": "model.boundary_condition.create", "params": {"name": "Thot", "type": "temperature", "target": {"set": "x1"}, "value": 120}},
 {"command": "model.boundary_condition.create", "params": {"name": "symx", "type": "symmetry", "target": {"set": "x0"}, "plane": "x"}},
 {"command": "model.boundary_condition.create", "params": {"name": "symy", "type": "symmetry", "target": {"set": "y0"}, "plane": "y"}},
 {"command": "model.boundary_condition.create", "params": {"name": "symz", "type": "symmetry", "target": {"set": "z0"}, "plane": "z"}},
 {"command": "model.step.create", "params": {"name": "Expand", "procedure": {"type": "coupled_temperature_displacement"}, "boundary_conditions": ["Tcold", "Thot", "symx", "symy", "symz"]}},
 {"command": "solve.static", "params": {"step": "Expand"}},
 {"command": "solve.probe", "params": {"step": "Expand", "at": [[100, 10, 10], [200, 10, 10], [200, 20, 20], [195, 10, 10]]}}
]
```

### Evidence

| point | T | u_x | expected | error |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| (100, 10, 10) | 70.000 | 0.030200 | 0.030000 | +0.67 % |
| (200, 10, 10) | 120 | 0.120200 | 0.120000 | +0.17 % |
| (200, 20, 20) | 120 | 0.118400 | 0.120000 | −1.33 % |
| (195, 10, 10) | 117.5 | 0.114275 | 0.114075 | +0.18 % |

`solve.static` reports `max_von_mises` = **29.24 MPa** (node 3585, on an end face); the probed interior points have 0.000 MPa.
The transverse displacements are exact (0.006, 0.012, 0.024 mm). With hex8, 20 × 2 × 2: u_x(200, 20, 20) = 0.118479 (−1.27 %),
max von Mises 21.09 MPa. Changing the mesh does not make the error go away, so it does not look like discretisation error.

### Expected behaviour

Steel, α = 1.2·10⁻⁵ K⁻¹, T_ref = 20 °C, L = 200 mm, b = h = 20 mm, T(x) = 20 + 100 x/L.
- Stresses: σ = 0 everywhere (a linear temperature field in an unconstrained body is compatible).
- u_x(x) = α · 100 · x² / (2L): u_x(100) = **0.030000 mm**, u_x(200) = **0.120000 mm** on the whole end face.
- u_y(200, y) = α · 100 · y: 0.012 mm at y = 10, 0.024 mm at y = 20.

### Investigation

- Possibly the nodes carrying the prescribed temperature (the two end faces) enter the thermal-strain load with a different
  temperature than the one reported, or the thermal load of the mid-side nodes on those faces is not consistent.
- Workaround seen: none (holding the temperature with convection instead was not tried).

### Version and platform

FieldCraft 0.8.1 (`fieldcraft-cli` from the Windows x64 release package, `mcp --headless`, CPU); Windows 11 Pro x64
