title: LES: wall models on interpolated (Bouzidi) walls, with the wall distance and normal from the true surface
body:
Part of the LES accuracy and stability tracking issue (#785). Depends on #732 (interpolated walls) and on a wall model that carries the stress it requests (#786).

## Gap

Interpolated bounce-back (Bouzidi, Firdaouss & Lallemand 2001; #732) places a no-slip wall at the true surface: each wall link carries the fraction q of the link inside the fluid. It is refused together with a wall model (`musker`, `musker_stress`, `spalding_bounce`, `spalding_bounce_halfway`), so wall-modelled LES on a curved body still uses the staircase wall. There:

- the wall distance the model sees is the staircase distance (Δx/2 for halfway, the node for the on-node form), not the distance from the first fluid node to the surface;
- the wall-normal direction is a lattice direction, not the surface normal;
- the stress is applied to staircase links, so its distribution over the surface follows the grid.

On grid-aligned walls (the channel, the square cylinder of #789) q = ½ everywhere and nothing changes. On a cylinder or a sphere the wall distance varies from 0 to more than one cell along the surface, so the model is evaluated at the wrong y⁺ on most of it.

## What is asked

A wall model evaluated on interpolated walls:

1. the wall distance of each wall cell from its links' fractions q (the distance to the surface along the surface normal), and the surface normal from the face-tagged surface, not from the lattice directions;
2. the model's velocity sampled at the matching point along that normal (interpolated), and the stress it returns applied through the interpolated links, so the force the flow carries equals the stress requested (the #786 criterion: carried and requested stress agree within the sampling error);
3. the moving-wall and momentum-exchange terms consistent with #732's Galilean-invariant force.

Methods come from papers only (e.g. Malaspinas & Sagaut 2014 for the reconstruction; published curved-wall wall-function LBM work, chosen and cited when this is picked up). No GPL code (OpenLB, Palabos, waLBerla).

## Acceptance

- Channel (q = ½): identical to the staircase wall model, bit for bit on CPU.
- Channel with walls at an arbitrary cell fraction (as #732's shifted channel): C_f from the carried drag within the #786 gate of Dean, independent of the shift.
- Pipe at Re_τ ≈ 1000 (curved wall, analytic friction law reference, e.g. Prandtl's for smooth pipes): carried C_f within the gate at N = 10–20 cells per radius, and the spread over N smaller than the staircase wall model's.
- 3D cylinder at Re 3900 (#787): report C_d against the published LES/experiment band with the wall model on interpolated walls, against the staircase wall model (#788: +80 %).

## Not in scope

The wall model's own carried-stress gap (#786) and the wall-row checkerboard of the halfway wall function (#794): this issue assumes a wall model that passes #786 on the channel first.

title: Provenance in every solve.fluid reply and run directory, and `fieldcraft-cli --version --verbose`
body:
### Problem

A long unattended run's result is often read days later, by someone who didn't start it. It may sit next to results from other builds, or from a GPU run. To reproduce or compare a result, they need to know exactly what produced it. Today:

- `solve.fluid`'s reply gives `backend` and `backend_choice` (what chose the backend), but not the build, the device behind `gpu`, or the thread count actually used.
- The build's commit is known only when the build named one (`FIELDCRAFT_BUILD_SHA`, set by packaging/env.sh and read by `crash::Build::current` in `crates/engine/src/crash.rs`). It's used in crash reports and solver-diagnostic records (#654), not in a successful reply. A plain `cargo build` records no commit.
- The GPU adapter, driver and limits are observed while the backend is prepared (`progress::BackendDiagnostic`, filled in `crates/lbm-gpu/src/native.rs`). They reach only diagnostic records.
- The checkpoint identity (`checkpoint::identity` in `crates/io/src/checkpoint.rs`) is computed and checked, but not reported. A reader can't tell which runs share a model and settings.
- `fieldcraft-cli --version` prints only the package version.

GPU results are deterministic per device and within a stated tolerance of the CPU. That's why the device belongs in the record. Across FieldCraft versions results may change by design, which is why the build belongs in it too.

### Proposal

`solve.fluid`'s reply gains a `provenance` object, and #907's `manifest.json` carries the same object:

- `version`, and `commit` when the build recorded one (otherwise `null`, never a guess). A build script falls back to `git rev-parse` when `FIELDCRAFT_BUILD_SHA` isn't set and a repository is present, and records whether the tree had changes;
- `target` (the target triple) and `profile` (debug or release), recorded at build time;
- `rustc`, the compiler version, recorded at build time;
- `backend`, and for the GPU the adapter, its graphics API and driver (from the existing `BackendDiagnostic`);
- `threads`, the thread count the CPU solve ran with;
- `checkpoint_identity`, the hex identity (for a GPU checkpoint, #912, it includes the device) when a checkpoint was used, so runs of the same model and settings can be matched.

`fieldcraft-cli --version --verbose` (or a `version` subcommand with `--json`) prints the same build fields for the binary. A command (for example `app.version`) returns them to scripts and MCP.

All values are gathered at build time or from data the run already has. Nothing in the solve changes. Build-time fields come from `env!`/`option_env!` set by a build script that does no network access and stays deterministic for a given tree.

Opt-in in the sense that results are untouched: the solution and stored results are byte-identical. Only the reply and the run directory gain fields.

### Acceptance criteria

- The reply's `provenance` is present on CPU and GPU runs, and in `manifest.json`. Its fields are documented in the command's params doc and in docs/features.md.
- A build without `FIELDCRAFT_BUILD_SHA` and without git reports `commit: null`, and the build still succeeds (crates.io and source-archive builds).
- `fieldcraft-cli --version --verbose` prints the fields, and a test checks its shape.
- The build script doesn't break wasm (`cargo xtask wasm`) or reproducible packaging.
- The stored results, and the solution's bits, are unchanged (a test compares a run's result before and after).

### Out of scope

- Signing or attesting results.
- Recording the host machine's identity, user or paths. Provenance names the build and the backend, not the person or the machine.
- Provenance for the other solvers. The same object can be added to them later.

title: Steady rule with averaging: a standard error and a stationarity check per monitor, and an optional target error
body:
### Problem

Turbulent and periodic flows never go steady. Their result is a mean, and a long unattended run needs to know when that mean is known well enough to stop. With averaging, the steady rule (`crates/lbm/src/steady.rs`) stops when the relative spread of each quantity's running mean over a window falls below the tolerance in two consecutive full windows. The report adds each quantity's mean, its root mean square about the mean, and its extremes (`steady::Average`). That isn't an uncertainty:

- a running mean over many samples changes little per window whether or not it has converged, so a long average passes the rule even when its error is large;
- a slowly drifting mean (a start-up transient that hasn't died out, a slow mode) also passes, because its change per window is small;
- the `rms` is the spread of the signal, not the error of its mean. Correlated samples make the error of the mean much larger than `rms / √n`.

The lbm crate already has bounded batch means with Student-t intervals and lag-correlation checks (`fieldcraft_lbm::statistics::Blocks`, `crates/lbm/src/statistics.rs`). The tests use it, but `solve.fluid`'s steady rule and reply don't.

### Proposal

For each monitored quantity under averaging, reported in `stop.averages`:

- a **batch-means standard error of the mean**, and its interval at a stated confidence, from the averaged samples. This reuses `statistics::Blocks`, with the block length chosen by a documented rule (a fixed number of blocks, or the shortest length whose block means pass the existing lag-correlation check). Fewer blocks than `statistics::MIN_BLOCKS` reports `null` with the reason, not a number;
- a **split-window stationarity check**: the averaged samples' first half against their second half, as the difference of the two halves' means relative to its combined standard error, with a pass/fail at a stated threshold. A drifting mean fails it.

An optional `target_error` on the averaging block (relative, or absolute in the quantity's display unit) stops the run, with `stop.reason` `converged` (or `steady`; to be settled in review), once every monitored mean's half-width is within it and every stationarity check passes, at a full-window boundary at or after `min_time`.

With #907's run directory, each monitor's current mean, standard error and stationarity go into `monitors.jsonl` at every sample, so a reader can watch the uncertainty fall.

Related: #911 lets a run whose mean hasn't reached `target_error` be extended on resume instead of started again.

Methods are cited in the module docs and in docs (batch means and the Student-t interval as `statistics.rs` already cites, plus a source for the split-window test).

Opt-in: without `target_error`, the new fields are added to the report, but the stop decision and the results are byte-identical to today's. The statistics are computed from the samples the monitors already take, so the solution is unaffected.

### Acceptance criteria

- On a synthetic series with known autocorrelation (an AR(1) process with a set coefficient), the reported standard error matches the analytical one within a stated tolerance. Treating the samples as independent would not.
- A series with a linear drift fails the stationarity check, and a stationary one passes it at the stated rate.
- A flow run with `target_error` stops when the criterion holds, not before. The same run without it is byte-identical to today's.
- A resume restores the accumulators, and a resumed run takes the same decision at the same step (`crates/lbm/tests/checkpoint.rs`).
- CPU and GPU take the decision at the same step, or the GPU's difference is stated within the backend's tolerance. The monitors already sample at the same chunk boundaries on both.
- Hostile input: `target_error` that's non-finite, zero or negative, or an averaging window too short for the minimum number of blocks. Each is refused before the solve, with tests.

### Out of scope

- Changing the existing tolerance rule or its defaults.
- Spectral or other estimators besides batch means.
- Deciding when the start-up transient ends. `averaging.start` stays the user's choice, and the stationarity check reports when it was too early.

title: solve.fluid estimate: regime warnings before the run (relaxation time, Mach, grid Reynolds, y⁺)
body:
Related: #913 (calibration in the same estimate reply). #908 checks the same quantities while the run goes; this issue checks them before it starts.

### Problem

A long unattended run should fail at submission, not hours in, when its settings are outside the scheme's sound range. And it should say up front when they're close to that range. Today:

- The setup refuses a lattice Mach number above `MAX_MACH` (0.3) and a relaxation time below `MIN_TAU` (0.505, or `MIN_TAU_TURBULENT` 0.5001 with a subgrid model), among other checks (`Setup::new` in `crates/lbm/src/setup.rs`).
- These checks run only when the solve starts. `"estimate": true` doesn't build the setup (`Memory::estimate` reads only the domain's shape), so an estimate can succeed for a step the solve then refuses.
- `tau` and `mach` appear only in the solved reply. Nothing reports how close a setting is to a limit, or the grid (cell) Reynolds number. With a wall model, the first-cell y⁺ is known only from the end-of-run warning (`wall::unresolved_wall`).

### Proposal

Every `"estimate": true` reply builds the `Setup` (`Setup::new`, with the obstacles triangulated as the solve does) without allocating the flow. So it refuses what the solve would refuse, and it reports a `regime` object:

- the relaxation time, with its distance from ½ and from the active `MIN_TAU`;
- the lattice Mach number against `MAX_MACH`;
- the grid Reynolds number;
- with a wall model, the expected first-cell y⁺ from a stated skin-friction estimate (cited in the module docs);
- `notices` for combinations the project already knows to be fragile:
  - settings within a stated margin of the setup's refusals;
  - combinations that open issues record.
  
  The list is kept in one place in code, and each entry cites its issue, so a fix removes its entry.

The solved reply carries the same `regime` object and adds its notices to `warnings`.

Opt-in in the sense that results are untouched: the solution and stored results are byte-identical. The estimate does more work (it triangulates the obstacles), and the reply gains fields.

### Acceptance criteria

- An estimate of a step the solve would refuse (Mach or τ out of range) returns that refusal, with the same message.
- A step within the stated margin of a limit gets its notice, and one well inside gets none.
- A wall-model step reports a y⁺ that agrees with the solved run's reported y⁺ within a stated tolerance on a test channel.
- Each entry in the fragile-combinations list has a test that triggers it.
- The estimate's added cost (triangulation, setup) stays bounded by the existing caps. A hostile step (huge cell counts, non-finite parameters) is refused as quickly as today.

### Out of scope

- Throughput and wall-time calibration (#913).
- Changing the setup's limits or the guard.
- Choosing settings automatically from the warnings.

title: solve.fluid estimate: a short calibration for throughput, wall time and output size
body:
Related: #914 (regime warnings in the same estimate reply). #907's `status.json` reports the live throughput and time left. #909's `max_seconds` is easier to choose with a projection.

### Problem

Before a long unattended run is queued, the person or script queuing it needs to know how long it will take and how much it will write: to request a scheduler time limit, to choose `checkpoint_every`, and to check that the disk will hold it. Today:

- `"estimate": true` returns only the memory estimate (`fluid_estimate` in `crates/engine/src/cmd/solve.rs`, `Memory::estimate` in `crates/lbm/src/memory.rs`): `flow_bytes`, `frame_bytes`, `total_bytes`, `bound_bytes`, `frames_that_fit` and the caps' ceilings. With a checkpoint path it adds a fixed note. It gives no throughput, wall time or checkpoint size.
- Measured throughput exists only in tests marked `#[ignore]` (`crates/lbm/tests/throughput.rs`, `crates/lbm-gpu/tests/throughput.rs`) and in tables in docs/manual/fluid/gpu.md, for the machines they were measured on. A user's machine, backend and thread count have no figure.
- A solved reply doesn't report its cell updates per second either, so a projection can't be checked afterwards.

### Proposal

`"calibrate": N` with `"estimate": true` (N a few dozen steps by default, capped in steps and in seconds). It builds the flow on the chosen backend and thread count, runs N steps, discards them, and returns:

- `cell_updates_per_second`, measured after a warm-up;
- `projected_seconds` for the planned steps, counting the history, frame and monitor readbacks the run will make. On the GPU those readbacks dominate small grids, as the manual's flow-past example shows;
- `checkpoint_bytes`, the serialized state's size from the same `RunState`/`Backend::checkpoint` code as a real save, when a checkpoint is given;
- `frame_bytes` for the whole run, as today.

The solved reply also gains `cell_updates_per_second` and its wall time, so a projection can be checked against the real run.

Opt-in: the calibration runs only when asked. A solved run's results are byte-identical; its reply gains two fields.

### Acceptance criteria

- On the CPU, a calibrated projection is within a stated factor of the measured wall time for a test run. That's a heavy test (`#[ignore = "heavy: …"]`), with a fast smoke test of the reply's shape in the trunk gate.
- `checkpoint_bytes` equals the size of the checkpoint the real run writes.
- The calibration's own cost is capped in steps and seconds, and both caps are tested.
- The calibration leaves the session's model and results unchanged.
- Hostile input: a calibration count of 0 or too large, a step with no cells, the GPU requested where none exists. Each is refused or falls back as `backend` already does, with tests.

### Out of scope

- Regime warnings (#914).
- A machine-wide benchmark database. The calibration measures this machine, now.
- Choosing `checkpoint_every` or `max_seconds` automatically.

title: Fluid checkpoints on the GPU backend
body:
This is the GPU fluid part of #653, which stays open for the explicit, nonlinear and transient heat solvers. Related: #910 (two generations) and #911 (extend on resume) should apply to GPU checkpoints once both exist. #909 needs a GPU checkpoint for a budget stop on the GPU to be resumable.

### Problem

The GPU backend is what makes long, fine fluid runs practical, and those are the runs most exposed to a restart: a lost device, a preempted or time-limited job, a reboot. Today they can't be checkpointed:

- `run_fluid` (`crates/engine/src/cmd/solve.rs`) refuses `checkpoint` unless the backend is `cpu`.
- `run_checkpointed` (`crates/lbm/src/solve.rs`) refuses a non-CPU backend.
- `Backend::checkpoint` (`crates/lbm/src/backend.rs`) refuses on device backends by default.

A GPU run can't be split into scheduled segments or survive a restart. A stop on the GPU loses the whole run.

### Proposal

- A device-backend checkpoint for `fieldcraft-lbm-gpu`. At a chunk boundary, it reads back the populations and the per-step device state (outlet, fan, thermal, subgrid and free-surface state, as for the CPU) and streams them through the same `RunState` archive and `CpuCheckpoint`-style store: atomic replacement, a SHA-256 over the content, verified on resume.
- The file has its own format tag. Its identity adds the device to what the CPU identity covers: adapter, graphics API, and the backend's layout and precision.
- A GPU checkpoint resumes on the same device. Resuming it on another device, or on the CPU, is refused, or at most allowed as a declared change outside the bit-identical guarantee (to be settled in review).
- The readback cost per save is measured in `crates/lbm-gpu/tests/throughput.rs` and stated in docs/manual/fluid/gpu.md.

Opt-in: only with a `checkpoint` path. Without one, GPU results are byte-identical to today's.

### Acceptance criteria

- On the GPU, a run interrupted and resumed on the same device gives the same bits as an uninterrupted run on that device. This covers each collision the GPU backend supports, heat, and steady windows with averaging. It's tested on lavapipe in CI, and the PR names the real GPU it also ran on.
- A GPU checkpoint offered to the CPU backend or to another adapter is refused with a message naming both (or follows the declared-change rule settled in review).
- A save that fails part-way leaves the previous checkpoint intact.
- The checkpoint's memory and size are checked against the session's bound before the run starts, as on the CPU.

### Out of scope

- Checkpoints for the other solvers (the rest of #653).
- Browser (WebGPU) checkpoints. The browser has no persistent native filesystem, and `CpuCheckpoint::new` refuses on wasm today.
- Moving a run between the GPU and the CPU bit for bit.

title: Fluid checkpoints: extend a run's length on resume
body:
Related: #910 (two checkpoint generations) and #912 (GPU checkpoints) change the same checkpoint format. #909's budget stops make segmented runs common. #915's statistics benefit from a longer averaging window. #653 is the original checkpoint issue.

### Problem

A long run is often planned in segments, or turns out to need more time than first planned: a mean that hasn't converged, or a transient that's still developing. Today a checkpointed run can't be extended. It has to start again from step 0.

- The checkpoint identity (`checkpoint::identity` in `crates/io/src/checkpoint.rs`) hashes the step's inputs (`results::definition_hash`, which covers the procedure's `end_time`/`steps`), the caps (`max_cells`, `max_steps`, `max_cell_updates`, `max_frame_bytes`) and the package version. So a longer `end_time` or `steps`, or a raised `max_steps`, is refused on resume as a different run. (Separately, `max_steps` may only be lowered below its default in any call. On resume, any change to it is refused.) Only the thread count and `checkpoint_every` may change today.
- Extending also changes things derived from the planned step count `total` in `run_checkpointed` (`crates/lbm/src/solve.rs`):
  - the frame schedule (`frame_step`);
  - the history interval (`total.div_ceil(MAX_HISTORY)`);
  - the validity sampler's interval (`validity::Sampler::new(total)`);
  - the averaging start, clamped to the step count (`SteadySetup`).

### Proposal

- `extend: true` on a resume allows a longer `end_time`/`steps` and a raised `max_steps`, as a declared change, as the thread count and cadence already are. The identity is split: the step's length and the step cap are checked separately from everything else, which must still match. Shortening, or changing anything else, is still refused.
- The flow state at every step stays the uninterrupted run's. Only the reporting schedules change: the frame and history schedules are recomputed for the new length from the resumed step on, so earlier frames and history samples are kept as they are. The reply records the original and new lengths and says how the schedules changed.
- Steady windows and running averages carry on across the extension unchanged.

Opt-in: without `extend`, the identity check and the results are byte-identical to today's. Checkpoints written before this change still resume as they do now.

### Acceptance criteria

- A run of N steps, resumed with `extend` to 2N, has the same flow state (populations, and the fields derived from them) at step 2N, bit for bit, as an uninterrupted 2N-step run. The test compares the final fields, not the frame lists.
- The extended run's frames and histories follow the documented schedule, with a test that covers steady windows and averaging spanning the extension.
- `extend` with a shorter length, a changed spacing, viscosity or boundary condition, or a lowered `max_steps` is refused with a message naming what changed.
- Resuming an extended checkpoint without `extend`, at its new length, works with no further declaration.
- The tests are in `crates/lbm/tests/checkpoint.rs` and `crates/engine` (the identity split).

### Out of scope

- Changing any other setting on resume, such as the time step or the monitors.
- GPU checkpoints (#912). Extending applies there once that lands.

title: Fluid checkpoints: keep the previous generation beside the newest
body:
Related: #911 (extending a run on resume) and #912 (GPU checkpoints) change the same checkpoint format. #909 writes a checkpoint on every clean stop. #653 is the original checkpoint issue.

### Problem

The CPU checkpoint from #653 (`crates/io/src/checkpoint.rs`) is what lets a long unattended run survive a restart. It keeps a single file:

- `CpuCheckpoint::save` atomically replaces the one file at `path`. The atomic replace protects against a torn write. It doesn't protect against a state that was written cleanly but is already bad: a run drifting towards instability saves its last sound-looking state over the only earlier one, and nothing older is left to go back to.
- A new run (`resume: false`) given the path of an existing checkpoint with the same identity starts from step 0. It overwrites that checkpoint at its first save, because `CpuCheckpoint::new` checks only the header. A script rerun by mistake, or a scheduler retrying a job without `resume`, throws away the saved state.

### Proposal

- Keep the previous checkpoint beside the newest (`<path>` and `<path>.prev`, or a numbered pair; to be settled in review). After each successful save, the older one is rotated, atomically, so a crash at any point leaves at least one complete, verified generation.
- Resume takes the newest by default. `resume: "previous"` takes the older one. The reply's `last_checkpoint` lists both generations, with their steps.
- A new run refuses to overwrite an existing checkpoint of the same identity unless told to (`overwrite: true`). The refusal says to resume or to pass `overwrite`.
- The checkpoint byte cap (the session's memory bound, `max_bytes`) counts both files, and the memory estimate's checkpoint note says so.
- With #907's run directory, `status.json` lists both generations.

Opt-in: the second generation is written only when asked (`checkpoint_keep: 2`, or a name settled in review). Without it, the files written and the results are byte-identical to today's. The overwrite refusal is a behaviour change for an existing workflow, so it's settled in review whether it's on by default.

### Acceptance criteria

- After a save that is then deliberately damaged, the default resume reports the damage. `resume: "previous"` resumes the older generation to the uninterrupted run's bits.
- A save that fails part-way leaves both generations intact. This is tested like `atomic_failure_keeps_the_last_valid_checkpoint_and_resume_verifies_every_byte`.
- A new run on an existing checkpoint without `overwrite` is refused, and with `overwrite` it starts over.
- The tests are in `crates/io/src/checkpoint.rs` and `crates/lbm/tests/checkpoint.rs`.
- Hostile input: a `.prev` file from another model, a missing `.prev`, or a `.prev` that's a directory is refused with a clear message, never silently used.

### Out of scope

- More than two generations, or keeping one every N saves.
- Extending a run on resume (#911) and GPU checkpoints (#912).
- Migrating checkpoints across FieldCraft versions. The identity includes the package version on purpose.

title: solve.fluid: a wall-clock budget, a stop file, signal handling in fieldcraft-cli, and a checkpoint on every clean stop
body:
### Problem

Batch schedulers and shared machines give a job a time limit. Near the limit they ask it to stop (SIGTERM, then SIGKILL after a grace period). Today a fluid run can't cooperate with that:

- Neither `solve.fluid` nor the solver has a time limit. `Limits` (`fieldcraft_lbm::Limits`) caps steps, cells, cell updates and frame bytes, but not seconds.
- Only the desktop's jobs and the control channel's `job.cancel` (`crates/ui-egui/src/control.rs`) can cancel a run. Cancelling takes effect at `progress::check()`, at the top of each advance chunk in `run_checkpointed` (`crates/lbm/src/solve.rs`). It returns `Error::Cancelled` without saving. The last checkpoint, written at a `checkpoint_every` multiple, is kept, and everything since is lost. `Session::execute` then restores the model, so the reply carries nothing of the run.
- `fieldcraft-cli` has no signal handling. Only the desktop app has one (`apps/fieldcraft/src/terminate.rs`). Its `run` subcommand installs no `Progress` that anything could cancel. So SIGTERM from a scheduler, or Ctrl-C, ends the process on the spot, mid-chunk.
- Rerunning the command with `resume: true` after the run has already completed restores the finished state and steps no further (the loop condition `k < total && !finished`). That's correct, but the reply doesn't say the run had already completed.

### Proposal

- `solve.fluid` gets `max_seconds` (wall-clock seconds from the start of this call), `stop_at` (a UTC time, RFC 3339) and `stop_file` (a path; when it exists, the run stops). All three are checked at advance-chunk boundaries, next to `progress::check()`. `stop_file` is the portable route, since Windows has no SIGTERM. It's checked at most once per second of wall-clock time, so a small grid doesn't stat a file every chunk.
- When a budget, the stop file or a cancel stops the run and a `checkpoint` path was given, it:
  1. saves at the current chunk boundary, through the existing atomic `CpuCheckpoint::save`;
  2. returns a normal reply (not an error), with `stop.reason` set to `budget` or `cancelled`, plus `last_checkpoint`, the steps done and the steps planned;
  3. keeps the frames and histories so far as the result, as a `diverged` stop does today.
  
  Without a checkpoint path, the result is the same partial result, and the reply says that nothing was saved.
- `fieldcraft-cli run`: SIGTERM and SIGINT (Ctrl-C and Ctrl-Break on Windows) request the same stop through the session's `Progress`. A second signal ends the process with the signal's default action, as `terminate.rs` does in the app. Headless `fieldcraft-cli mcp` gets the same handling.
- Rerunning the same command with `resume: true` continues from the saved step. If the checkpoint is of a run that already completed, the reply says so (`already_complete: true`) and does no work.
- With #907's run directory, `status.json` records `budget` or `cancelled` and the checkpoint. #907's exit codes tell these stops apart from completion and failure.

The decision to stop depends on wall-clock time, which isn't deterministic. The stop always falls on a chunk boundary, though, and the saved state is the uninterrupted run's state at that step. So resuming gives the uninterrupted run's bits.

Opt-in: without these parameters and without a signal, results are byte-identical to today's. The solver part doesn't depend on #907. Related: #910 keeps the previous checkpoint beside the one a stop writes, #911 lets a stopped segment be extended, and #913 projects the wall time to choose `max_seconds` from.

### Acceptance criteria

- A run stopped by each of the four routes resumes to the same bits as an uninterrupted run: `max_seconds`, `stop_at`, `stop_file`, and cancel (from `job.cancel` and from a signal to `fieldcraft-cli run`). The tests stop at a chosen step through a test hook rather than real time, so they're fast and deterministic. The signal test runs the CLI binary on Unix.
- A stop between two `checkpoint_every` multiples loses no steps: the saved step is the step reached.
- A second signal ends the process. A test checks the exit status.
- `resume: true` on a completed checkpoint returns `already_complete: true` and advances no step.
- Hostile input: negative, zero or non-finite `max_seconds`, a `stop_at` that doesn't parse or is in the past, a `stop_file` outside the read root. Each is refused or stops at once, as documented, with tests.

### Out of scope

- GPU checkpoints (#912, the GPU part of #653). Until then, a budget stop on the GPU returns the partial result without a checkpoint and says so.
- Other solvers' budgets.
- Choosing `max_seconds` automatically from a scheduler's environment variables.

title: solve.fluid: health samples with warn and stop limits, and a stop on sustained exponential growth
body:
### Problem

On a long unattended run, a stop at step 2 000 is worth more than an `Error::Unstable` at step 900 000, and much more than a run that finishes with a field nobody should use. Today:

- The only hard stop is the blow-up guard in `Flow::step` (`crates/lbm/src/flow.rs`). It trips when the lattice speed passes `MAX_LATTICE_SPEED` (0.5) or a density stops being a positive number, or, with heat, when a temperature stops being a number. By then the run is already lost. Without a steady rule it's an error (`run_checkpointed`, `crates/lbm/src/solve.rs`). With one, the run ends as `diverged` with the frames so far.
- The steady rule's divergence limit (`crates/lbm/src/steady.rs`) looks at a monitor's relative spread per window. It doesn't see a local fault far from the monitors.
- The reply's `validity` block (`crates/lbm/src/validity.rs`) reports density-departure and local-Mach extrema. It only measures field reads the run makes anyway (frames, steady-monitor samples, the final field), so its cadence depends on the frame count and the steady rule. It gives no cell, has no limit that acts on the run, and is reported only at the end. Mass drift, the effective relaxation time and the wall y⁺ appear only as end-of-run warnings (`COMPRESSIBILITY_WARNING`, `rheology::Clamps::warning`, `wall::unresolved_wall`).

A run can therefore stay finite while it sits outside the scheme's valid range for its whole length, or grow steadily towards the guard. Nobody learns this until the reply arrives.

### Proposal

A `health` block on the fluid step (or on `solve.fluid`; to be settled in review), sampling every `every` steps at an advance-chunk boundary:

| Quantity | Reported |
|---|---|
| largest local Mach number (√3·\|u\| in lattice units) | value, cell, step |
| largest density departure \|ρ/ρ₀ − 1\| | value, cell, step |
| total mass drift relative to the start (net of what the open faces carry in and out, where that balance is defined) | value, step |
| smallest effective relaxation time, with a subgrid model or shear-dependent viscosity | value, cell, step |
| wall y⁺ range, with a wall model | min, max, step |

Each quantity has an optional `warn` and `stop` limit. A warn adds one warning to the reply, at its first crossing, with the count of later crossings. A stop ends the run.

A second rule stops on sustained exponential growth. For a chosen quantity (local Mach by default), it fits a growth rate to the log of the samples over a window. When the rate stays positive and above a threshold for the whole window, it projects the step at which the quantity would cross its hard limit, and stops when that step is within a horizon. The fit and the thresholds come from a cited source in the module docs.

A stop by health is a sound stop:
- the last checkpoint stays, and no checkpoint is written from the unhealthy state;
- the reply's `stop` names the rule, the quantity, its value, the cell (as a position in SI and as indices), and the step;
- the frames so far are kept and a last frame is added, as a `diverged` stop does today;
- `execution` is `diverged` (or a new `health` reason; to be settled in review), and the run directory from #907 records it in `status.json` and every sample in `health.jsonl`.

Opt-in: without a `health` block nothing is sampled, and results are byte-identical to today's.

Related: #914 reports the same quantities' expected values before the run starts. #907 receives the samples.

### Acceptance criteria

- A seeded unstable case (for example an inlet speed raised until the guard trips) stops by the growth rule well before `Error::Unstable` would, with the step and margin in the test.
- A stable case from the existing test set never trips it, with the default thresholds, over its full length.
- The samples are read-only: the bits don't change with sampling on. This is tested the way `checkpoints_split_existing_advance_chunks_without_changing_bits` tests added chunk boundaries, including a sampling interval that's coprime with the history and progress cadences.
- A resume restores the health state (window, first-warning flags), and a resumed run takes the same stop decision at the same step. This is covered in `crates/lbm/tests/checkpoint.rs`.
- On the GPU backend it either works, with a stated readback cost per sample measured in the GPU throughput tests and given in the manual, or it's refused with a clear message.
- Hostile input: non-finite or negative limits, an interval of 0 or above the step count, a growth window longer than the run. All are refused, with tests.

### Out of scope

- Changing `MAX_LATTICE_SPEED`, the setup's refusals or the end-of-run warnings.
- Changing the `validity` block. It stays a descriptive report. Health is a separate, opt-in rule that acts on the run.
- Fixing any particular unstable configuration. This issue only detects them earlier.

title: solve.fluid: an optional run directory with live status, monitor and health logs, and the final reply
body:
### Problem

A long fluid run is often started by a scheduler, a batch queue or a script and left alone. Nobody watches it, and the process may end at any point. Today such a run leaves nothing an outside process can read while it runs or after it dies:

- `solve.fluid` returns one reply, at the end (`run_fluid` in `crates/engine/src/cmd/solve.rs`). The monitor history (`stop.history`) and the averages live in memory until then, and in the checkpoint when there is one, in a binary format meant only for resuming.
- The step count is reported through `fieldcraft_model::progress` (`stage`/`count` in `run_checkpointed`, `crates/lbm/src/solve.rs`). Only a host that holds the command's `Progress` can read it: the desktop's jobs and the control channel's `job.status`. `fieldcraft-cli run` and headless `fieldcraft-cli mcp` have no such reader.
- `fieldcraft-cli run` prints the `model.info` summary at the end, not the solve's reply (`run` in `apps/fieldcraft-cli/src/main.rs`). It exits 0 or 1 (`ExitCode::SUCCESS`/`FAILURE`), so a run that stopped as `diverged` exits 0 just like one that completed.
- A failed or stopped solve leaves a solver-diagnostic record (#654, `crates/engine/src/solver_diagnostic.rs`). That's a post-mortem of a failure. It isn't the state of a run that's still going, or of one that was killed.

### Proposal

An optional `run_dir` parameter on `solve.fluid`, a folder checked like `checkpoint` (`Session::checked_path` with `Access::Write`, so it stays inside the automation write root when one is set). It holds:

- `manifest.json`, written once at the start: the command, its parameters, the step, the cell count, the planned steps and the provenance from #916.
- `status.json`, replaced atomically at reporting events (at most once per advance chunk, with a minimum interval in wall-clock seconds so small grids don't write on every chunk):
  - `state`: `running`, `completed`, `steady`, `diverged`, `unstable`, `budget` or `cancelled` (later issues add their reasons to this list);
  - `step`, `planned_steps`, `flow_time`;
  - `cell_updates_per_second` and `estimated_seconds_left`, measured over a recent window;
  - the last checkpoint's `step` and `path`, when there is a checkpoint;
  - the solver-diagnostic record's path, when one was written.
- `monitors.jsonl`, appended: one line per monitor sample, the same values the reply's `stop.history` carries, in the same display units.
- `health.jsonl`, appended by #908.

`cell_updates_per_second` here is the live counterpart of #913's calibrated figure.
- `reply.json` at the end: the reply exactly as the command returns it. On an error, it holds the error and the last checkpoint.

`fieldcraft-cli run` gets documented exit codes for a script whose last solve ended as completed (or steady), diverged or unstable, stopped by a budget (#909), or cancelled. They go in the CLI usage text and in docs/.

The files are written for other programs to read. Their fields and units are documented, and every file carries a `format` version. Appends are whole lines, so a reader never sees half a record.

Opt-in: without `run_dir`, nothing is written and the reply and results are byte-identical to today's.

### Acceptance criteria

- A reader can follow a run from the directory alone: its state, its progress, its monitors, and how and where it ended.
- Killing the process at any moment leaves parseable files: `status.json` whole (the old or the new version), `*.jsonl` with whole lines only, and at most one partial trailing line, which a reader skips and a test covers.
- The solution's bits don't change with `run_dir` on. A test compares the result of a run with and without it, the way `crates/lbm/tests/checkpoint.rs` compares interrupted and uninterrupted runs.
- `run_dir` with `resume: true` continues the same directory: the appended files go on from the resumed step without duplicate lines.
- Hostile input: a path outside the write root, a path that's a file, an unwritable folder, an existing directory from another model. Each is refused before the solve starts, with a test in `hostile_params_never_panic`'s style.
- The exit codes are tested in `apps/fieldcraft-cli`.

### Out of scope

- Health sampling (#908), budgets and signals (#909), statistical stopping (#915) and provenance (#916): this issue gives them a place to write.
- Streaming frames or fields into the directory. Results stay in the project.
- A network endpoint for status. The control channel already serves the desktop app.
- Other solvers (`solve.explicit`, `solve.heat`, …). The format should allow them later.

title: Automatic volume meshing with a hex preference and quality requirements
body:
### Current behaviour

FieldCraft exposes structured hex, octree and tetrahedral meshing as separate commands. An agent that needs an all-Hex8 mesh with stated quality limits has to choose routes, check each candidate and handle mesh replacement itself.

### What you need and why

Provide one volume-meshing command that prefers hexahedra and reports the method used, achieved quality and actionable retry parameters. For example, on the SolidCraft sensor lid, an exploratory run rejected the standard extrusion partition (minimum scaled Jacobian 0.164, maximum edge ratio 85,310) and accepted an alternate partition at the same thresholds (0.342 and 4.84). An MCP client applied the returned partition change.

### Expected behaviour

- Expose `mesh.volume.auto` through the shared command layer and MCP. Prefer existing structured and octree routes. A restricted six-Tet4 fan recombination fallback may produce mixed cells.
- Report Hex8 fractions by count and volume, the selected method and candidate rejections. Let callers require all Hex8 or request a minimum hex fraction by volume.
- Apply explicit quality requirements to every requested body before replacing the current mesh. Return an unmet result and retry parameters where available.
- Verify the routing and retry contract with original SolidCraft geometry and bounded cases. Report failures alongside successes. Document linear-static FEA measurements with displacement, stress, free equations and solve time.

The scope is automatic meshing and explicit acceptance. General parameterization-based hex generation remains open in #875, and the octree fillet-stress investigation remains open in #876.

I have exploratory code and original before/after renders. Could a maintainer confirm whether this scope is welcome and open the issue for assignment before I submit the PR?

### References

- [Pellerin et al., tet-to-hex candidate identification and compatibility](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.cad.2018.05.004). The proposed matcher uses a restricted six-tet fan search.
- [Ray et al., parameterization-based hex-dominant meshing](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.cad.2018.04.012). Background for #875.

title: hex: the round-disk O-grid's quality depends on its rim count (best at 16; 20 gives 0.776)
body:
The round-disk O-grid's quality depends strongly on the rim node count, and 16 is its best count. Measured on its own (smallest hex8 scaled Jacobian vs rim nodes): 12 → 0.805, 16 → 0.831, 20 → 0.776, 24 → 0.781, 28 → 0.812, 32 → 0.785.

With the chordal curvature floor (#898) the rim counts follow the geometry instead of a fixed 16 per circle, so this shows up in the corpus: analytic-torus (r = 8 section, 20 rim divisions at δ = 0.109) drops from 0.829 to 0.773, and pinhole-block's hex20 from 0.424 to 0.377 (hex8 improves 0.381 → 0.463).

**Expected:** the O-grid's quality is roughly independent of the rim count (a monotone or flat curve), so the floor's counts need no rounding toward 16. Likely places to look: the square core's size and placement relative to the rim count (core side vs rim spacing, the ¼/½ offsets tried), the core's node count per side when the rim count is not a multiple of 4·k, and the radial spacing between core and rim.

Restore analytic-torus to ≥ 0.829 and pinhole-block hex20 to ≥ 0.424 with the fix, and add a unit test sweeping the rim count 12..=32 with a floor on the worst quality.

title: tests red on develop since the solidcore kernel (d0242f6d): tet_metric_547, a fillet's nodes on its torus
body:
### Observed failure

`cargo test -p fieldcraft-testkit --test tet_metric_547` fails on `develop` (d4b72bd5) on Linux x86_64. It fails in every run, and it fails in `cargo xtask ci` as well:

```text
thread 'sphere_on_plate_report_and_quality_agree' panicked at crates/testkit/tests/tet_metric_547.rs:35:9:
linear: {"inadmissible":0,"max_dihedral":139.8290063444604,"mean_radius_ratio":0.7730190733195966,"mean_scaled_jacobian":0.5890156256281958,"min_dihedral":20.432448481025915,"min_radius_ratio":0.24163612289191766,"min_scaled_jacobian":0.2207697433733627,"slivers":0,"tets":19630}
```

### Reproduction

```sh
git switch --detach d0242f6d   # or develop
cargo test --profile ci --locked -p fieldcraft-testkit --test tet_metric_547
```

### Evidence

Bisected: it passes at 0474c3c9 and fails at d0242f6d ("geometry: SolidCraft at 5e33828 (solidcore kernel), adopting its face names").

### Expected behaviour

`cargo xtask ci` is green on `develop`.

### Investigation

d0242f6d accepts the drop on purpose. Its message says sphere-on-plate's "tet min dihedral 35.2° to 18.0°, its octree stops at its limit: the needle facets SolidCraft's tessellation leaves on the trimmed sphere, tangency-labs/solidcraft#14915", and it re-blesses `tests/corpus/sphere-on-plate/fixture.json` to match. `crates/testkit/tests/tet_metric_547.rs` still asserts `min_dihedral > 30.0` and `min_scaled_jacobian >= 0.3` for the same part at size 4, and it was not updated. So either the test's bounds follow the new fixture until solidcraft#14915 is fixed, or the test is ignored until then. That is your call. The test's other checks (the report and `mesh.quality` agree) still hold.

### Version and platform

`develop` d4b72bd5 (Rust 1.98.0), Fedora 44 x86_64 VM, 16 vCPU. The test runs on the CPU, so the GPU does not matter.

title: Beam sections from section properties (area, I_y, I_z, J, shear areas)
body:
### Current behaviour

A beam section's profile can only be a shape: `rectangle`, `circle`, `pipe`, `i` or `box`, with the properties computed from it. Section properties cannot be given directly. This rules out:
- rolled sections from tables, for example I/H sections with root radii (EN 10365), channels and angles;
- a frame model brought over from another program, which carries only A, I and J.

### What you need and why

Steel frames are designed with the table values of rolled sections. Comparing a frame analysis with another frame program needs exactly that program's section values. A shape that only approximates them (an `i` without root radii) gives a different I_t and different shear areas.

### Expected behaviour

A `general` beam profile that takes the properties directly: area, I_y, I_z, torsion constant J and shear areas along y and z, each validated as positive and finite. Inside FieldCraft it would behave like the other profiles, with the same `BeamProperties` and the same element, and the deck writers would map it to their general beam section.

We have this as a small patch in our copy of `fieldcraft-model`: the `BeamProfile::General` variant, with `name`, `validate`, `area`, `properties` and the unit conversion in `convert.rs`, about 40 lines. We use it to cross-check frames against another program (PyNite): reactions are equal and moments agree within 0.4 %. Our copy does not include the `io`/`decks` crates, so the deck writers would still be open. I can turn it into a pull request against `develop` if you want this.

### Pictures

_No response_

### References

EN 10365 (dimensions and section properties of hot-rolled I and H sections). The beam element itself is unchanged.

title: Curved quadratic shells: MITC8 and MITC6-a, with distorted multi-element patch tests
body:
### Current behaviour

The solver's shell elements are the flat four-node MITC4 and three-node MITC3; curved shells are approximated by facets. The model has eight-node quadrilateral and six-node triangle kinds, but there is no curved quadratic shell formulation for them.

### What you need and why

Following the review of #861, I would like to contribute the two curved quadratic shells, MITC8 and MITC6-a, as the eighth piece of the suggested order, and to agree on the scope here first. The implementation exists on my fork; it will be rebuilt as linear commits on current `develop`, with the distorted multi-element patch tests you asked for added before anything is sent.

A curved quadratic shell follows a cylinder or a doubly curved panel with far fewer elements than facets do.

### Expected behaviour

Proposed as two PRs, one element each:

1. **MITC8.** Eight-node quadrilateral with curved geometry and nodal directors, six degrees of freedom per node, mixed interpolation of the in-layer and transverse shear strain components after Bathe and Dvorkin, homogeneous sections, consistent mass. Linear static and frequency steps.
2. **MITC6-a.** Six-node triangle with the tying scheme of Lee and Bathe, on the same geometry and section interface.

Each PR brings, for its element: membrane and bending patch tests on distorted multi-element patches, in the manner of the existing `shell_membrane_patch_test` and `shell_bending_patch_test`; rigid-body modes; and curved-shell cases from the literature (Scordelis–Lo roof, pinched hemisphere, twisted beam) under new oracle ids. The frozen `nafems-le7` case is left exactly as it is; a shell variant gets an id of its own.

Not in this piece: nonlinear shells, harmonic and transient steps, layered sections (they follow the composites piece), folded junctions, and any change to deck export.

Points for your sign-off:

- One element per PR, MITC8 first: is that the split you want?
- For the distorted patches, would you like the same tolerances as the two existing patch tests, and is there a distortion you want covered in particular?
- How should the new oracle cases be named?

### Pictures

_No response_

### References

- K.-J. Bathe, E. N. Dvorkin, "A formulation of general shell elements — the use of mixed interpolation of tensorial components", Int. J. Numer. Methods Eng. 22 (1986) 697–722, doi:10.1002/nme.1620220312.
- P.-S. Lee, K.-J. Bathe, "Development of MITC isotropic triangular shell finite elements", Comput. Struct. 82 (2004) 945–962, doi:10.1016/j.compstruc.2004.02.004.
- R. H. MacNeal, R. L. Harder, "A proposed standard set of problems to test finite element accuracy", Finite Elem. Anal. Des. 1 (1985) 3–20, doi:10.1016/0168-874X(85)90003-4.

title: Composites: material orientations, layups, lamination stiffness and ply results on flat shells (M18)
body:
### Current behaviour

Materials can be orthotropic and shell sections are homogeneous through the thickness. There is no material orientation, no layup, no laminate stiffness and no ply result. ROADMAP lists these under M18 as planned.

### What you need and why

Following the review of #856–#861, I would like to contribute composites and orientations as the seventh piece of the suggested order. M18 has no owner sign-off yet, so this issue is to agree on the scope before any code is sent. The implementation exists on my fork; it will be rebuilt as linear commits on current `develop`.

Laminated plates and shells need three things to be analysed at all: a declared material frame, the plies in order, and stresses per ply in material axes.

### Expected behaviour

Proposed as two PRs, each with its own tests:

1. **Orientations and layups.** Material orientations as rectangular and cylindrical frames, projected onto the shell reference surface. Layups as ordered plies (material, thickness, angle) with an offset. Classical lamination stiffness (A, B, D), transverse shear stiffness and mass moments. A command that returns the section properties. Named refusals: a degenerate direction, a point on the cylinder axis, a missing material, a missing density where mass is needed.
2. **Ply results.** Stresses and strains in material axes at the bottom and top of each ply, kept one-sided at ply interfaces, and first-ply failure indices from declared strengths: maximum stress, Tsai–Hill, Tsai–Wu and Hashin (1980). No stiffness degradation.

On the existing flat shells (MITC4, MITC3), in linear static and frequency steps.

Verification: closed forms of classical lamination theory (A, B, D of standard laminates, pure bending, Navier solutions for simply supported laminated plates, static and frequency) as theory cases; a NAFEMS laminated-shell strength benchmark as a published-benchmark case; one published measurement of cantilever-plate frequencies as an experiment case.

Not in this piece: thermal resultants, progressive damage, delamination and interlaminar stresses, Puck and LaRC criteria, strength allowables, and the curved quadratic shells, which have their own issue.

Points for your sign-off:

- Is this the first M18 scope you want: orientations, layups, lamination stiffness, ply results and first-ply indices on flat shells?
- Should orientations on solid elements come with PR 1, or later?
- Is the NAFEMS laminate case a gate for the PR, or informative?

### Pictures

_No response_

### References

- A. T. Nettles, *Basic Mechanics of Laminated Composite Plates*, NASA Reference Publication 1351, 1994.
- R. M. Jones, *Mechanics of Composite Materials*, 2nd ed., Taylor & Francis, 1999.
- S. W. Tsai, E. M. Wu, "A general theory of strength for anisotropic materials", J. Compos. Mater. 5 (1971) 58–80, doi:10.1177/002199837100500106.
- Z. Hashin, "Failure criteria for unidirectional fiber composites", J. Appl. Mech. 47 (1980) 329–334, doi:10.1115/1.3153664.
