title: Solver: parallel assembly with fixed row ownership, bit-identical to serial
body:
### Current behaviour

Element matrices of several families are already computed in parallel, but they are scattered into the sparse matrix one element after another, in a fixed order. On large solid models the serial scatter dominates assembly time.

### What you need and why

Following the review of #860, this is the third of the solver-speed pieces, on its own issue: parallel assembly of the stiffness and mass matrices with the serial result reproduced bit for bit. The implementation exists on my fork; it will be rebuilt as linear commits on current `develop`.

### Expected behaviour

One small PR:

- Element matrices are computed in bounded rounds; rows are divided among fixed owners, and each owner adds the contributions to its rows in the same element-label and local-node order as the serial path. No atomics and no partial sums that depend on the worker count.
- Stiffness and mass matrices equal the serial ones bit for bit, including repeated nodes, and the first error reported is the same one.
- Covered first: solid elements with consistent and lumped mass. Families not yet covered keep the serial path, named in the PR.
- Tests: bit equality with the serial matrices for 1, 2 and 7 threads for every matrix kind covered.
- Before and after assembly time in the PR, on models generated from the repository.

No environment variables and no stderr output in library code. The multiple right-hand-side solve is left to #807.

Point for your sign-off:

- Is solids first, with the other families kept serial until each has its own equality test, the split you want, or should beams and shells be in the same PR?

### Pictures

_No response_

### References

- T. J. R. Hughes, *The Finite Element Method: Linear Static and Dynamic Finite Element Analysis*, Prentice-Hall, 1987 (assembly).
- T. A. Davis, *Direct Methods for Sparse Linear Systems*, SIAM, 2006.

title: Solver: symbolic column counts in parallel, identical for any thread count
body:
### Current behaviour

After the elimination tree is built, the symbolic factorisation walks the row subtrees one column at a time and accumulates the column counts serially. The numeric supernodal updates already run in parallel, so on large models this serial pass is a visible part of the set-up time.

### What you need and why

Following the review of #860, this is the second of the solver-speed pieces, on its own issue: the symbolic column counts in parallel, with the result unchanged. The implementation exists on my fork; it will be rebuilt as linear commits on current `develop`.

### Expected behaviour

One small PR:

- The columns are split into a fixed number of contiguous ranges; each range counts its reaches independently through `fieldcraft-parallel`; the counts are merged in range order.
- The elimination tree, the column counts, the symbolic pattern, the factor-entry estimate and the factor-limit refusal are identical to the serial pass for every thread count.
- Tests: equality with the serial pass for 1, 2 and 7 threads on structured and unstructured patterns built in the test, including the refusal at the factor limit.
- Before and after time of the symbolic stage in the PR, on models generated from the repository.

No environment variables and no stderr output in library code. The multiple right-hand-side solve is left to #807.

Point for your sign-off:

- Is a fixed range count as a constant in the code acceptable, or would you rather derive it from the matrix size?

### Pictures

_No response_

### References

- J. W. H. Liu, "The role of elimination trees in sparse factorization", SIAM J. Matrix Anal. Appl. 11 (1990) 134–172.
- T. A. Davis, *Direct Methods for Sparse Linear Systems*, SIAM, 2006.

title: Solver: a deterministic multilevel nested-dissection ordering as a third candidate
body:
### Current behaviour

`fill_reducing_order` computes two nested-dissection orderings, coordinate bisection and graph dissection from a level structure, and keeps the one with fewer factor entries (#585). There is no multilevel candidate, so on large unstructured meshes both separators can be far from the best available.

### What you need and why

Following the review of #860, I would like to contribute the solver-speed work as separate pieces, each on its own issue. This is the first: a multilevel nested-dissection ordering as a third candidate. The implementation exists on my fork; it will be rebuilt as linear commits on current `develop`, without the experiment switches and diagnostics you pointed out.

A smaller factor is the largest single lever on direct-solve time and memory for big tetrahedral models.

### Expected behaviour

One PR:

- Multilevel nested dissection: heavy-edge coarsening, an initial separator on the coarsest graph, boundary refinement with locked moves and best-prefix rollback while uncoarsening, bounded leaves ordered by approximate minimum degree. Implemented from the papers below; no external partitioner.
- Deterministic: fixed visit order and starts, ties by node index, no randomness, no dependence on the thread count. Work is shared only through `fieldcraft-parallel`.
- `fill_reducing_order` keeps whichever of the three candidates has the fewest factor entries, with a stable rule on ties, so a model is never ordered worse than today.
- Explicit caps on levels and refinement passes.
- Tests: valid permutations on structured and unstructured meshes built in the test; identical ordering and solve results for 1, 2 and 7 threads; the fallback when the candidate is not better.
- Before and after factor entries and factorisation time in the PR, on models generated from the repository.

No environment variables and no stderr output in library code. The multiple right-hand-side solve is left to #807.

Points for your sign-off:

- Is "fewest factor entries" still the selection rule you want with three candidates, or should it weigh an operation count?
- Which repository models would you like the before and after numbers on?

### Pictures

_No response_

### References

- G. Karypis, V. Kumar, "A fast and high quality multilevel scheme for partitioning irregular graphs", SIAM J. Sci. Comput. 20 (1998) 359–392.
- C. M. Fiduccia, R. M. Mattheyses, "A linear-time heuristic for improving network partitions", 19th Design Automation Conference, 1982, 175–181.
- P. R. Amestoy, T. A. Davis, I. S. Duff, "An approximate minimum degree ordering algorithm", SIAM J. Matrix Anal. Appl. 17 (1996) 886–905.
- A. George, "Nested dissection of a regular finite element mesh", SIAM J. Numer. Anal. 10 (1973) 345–363.

title: Bolt pretension on a cut section, by exact constraint elimination (M7)
body:
### Current behaviour

There is no pretension section, no pretension control and no way to impose a bolt preload on a solid bolt or to read back its section force. ROADMAP (M7) lists pretension as planned, with the nonlinear steps.

### What you need and why

Following the review of #859, I would like to contribute bolt pretension as its own piece, and to agree on its scope here first. The implementation exists on my fork; it will be rebuilt as linear commits on current `develop`, without the nonlinear-solver edits, which you asked to review separately.

A preloaded bolt is the usual starting state of a bolted fixture: the clamp force is applied first, the bolt is then locked at its length, and the following steps see the preloaded assembly.

### Expected behaviour

One PR:

- A named pretension section on a planar cut through a solid bolt, with one scalar control degree of freedom for the cut adjustment.
- Three controls: a prescribed force, a prescribed adjustment, and a lock at the current adjustment for the following step.
- The cut relation `u⁺ − u⁻ = n q` enforced by exact constraint elimination, so no penalty stiffness and nothing to tune; the conjugate section force recovered from equilibrium.
- Commands to create the section, set the control and query adjustment and section force; named refusals (not a plane, cut not conforming, conflicting constraints, control point reused) that leave the model unchanged; hostile parameters.
- Linear static steps only. With zero force the results equal those of the uncut mesh bit for bit. Results identical for 1, 2 and 7 threads.
- Tests against closed forms: a two-element bar (`q = F L / (E A)`, `U = F q / 2`), force balance across the cut and at the supports, the lock reproducing the adjustment exactly.

Not in this PR: any change to the nonlinear solver, and frequency or harmonic steps on the preloaded state. Those would be follow-ups, the second after the harmonic piece.

Points for your sign-off:

- May the cut lie inside a continuous mesh (the section splits the nodes on an internal planar face itself), or should the first PR take only a pair of coincident faces?
- Where would you like the nonlinear integration discussed: a follow-up issue after this one lands?

### Pictures

_No response_

### References

- R. D. Cook, D. S. Malkus, M. E. Plesha, R. J. Witt, *Concepts and Applications of Finite Element Analysis*, 4th ed., Wiley, 2002 (constraints by transformation of the equations).
- J. Kim, J.-C. Yoon, B.-S. Kang, "Finite element analysis and modeling of structure with bolted joints", Appl. Math. Model. 31 (2007) 895–911.

title: Harmonic response: complex LDLᵀ, direct and modal steady-state steps (M16)
body:
### Current behaviour

The structural solver has linear static, frequency (Lanczos) and buckling steps and a real symmetric-indefinite LDLᵀ (#150). There is no complex factorisation, no steady-state harmonic step and no complex result. ROADMAP lists harmonic response under M16 as planned.

### What you need and why

Following the review of #856–#861, I would like to contribute the harmonic stack as the first piece of the suggested order, and to agree on its scope here before sending any code. The implementation exists on my fork; it will be rebuilt as linear commits on current `develop`.

Harmonic response is what a vibration fixture or a bracket on a shaker is checked with: displacement, acceleration and stress amplitudes and phases over a frequency band, with damping.

### Expected behaviour

Proposed as three PRs, each with its own tests:

1. **Complex symmetric LDLᵀ.** A supernodal factorisation of `K − ω²M + iωC` on interleaved complex storage, with deterministic pivoting and a reported relative residual; a singular or unsupported system is a named error. Checked against the equivalent real formulation in tests.
2. **Harmonic step and `solve.harmonic`, direct method.** Frequency lists and ranges, Rayleigh and structural damping, load phase; complex nodal results with amplitude and phase. Oracle cases with closed forms: a single-degree-of-freedom oscillator, a reciprocal two-mass system, a cantilever.
3. **Modal method.** Mode superposition with load-dependent residual vectors, reproducing the direct result within a stated tolerance; reuse of a modal basis only for an identical input, with the cached basis counted against the session limits, as asked on #860; the NAFEMS forced-vibration benchmark 5H as a published-benchmark case.

Throughout: results identical for 1, 2 and 7 threads, `libm` for every result-producing function, no environment switches, no stderr diagnostics in library code.

Not in this piece: random response, transient and response spectrum, fatigue, pretension. They follow in the order you gave.

Points for your sign-off:

- Should the residual vectors come with PR 3, or be a PR of their own?
- For the cached modal basis: is counting its bytes against the session limit and refusing (rather than evicting) at the limit the behaviour you want?
- For 5H I would cite the NAFEMS publication directly. Is that the source you accept for it?

### Pictures

_No response_

### References

- J. R. Bunch, "Stable algorithms for solving symmetric and skew-symmetric systems", Bull. Aust. Math. Soc. 26 (1982) 107–119, doi:10.1017/S0004972700005621.
- C. Ashcraft, R. G. Grimes, J. G. Lewis, "Accurate symmetric indefinite linear equation solvers", SIAM J. Matrix Anal. Appl. 20 (1998) 513–561, doi:10.1137/S0895479896296921.
- D. Day, M. A. Heroux, "Solving complex-valued linear systems via equivalent real formulations", SIAM J. Sci. Comput. 23 (2001) 480–498, doi:10.1137/S1064827500372262.
- E. L. Wilson, M.-W. Yuan, J. M. Dickens, "Dynamic analysis by direct superposition of Ritz vectors", Earthquake Eng. Struct. Dyn. 10 (1982) 813–821, doi:10.1002/eqe.4290100606.
- R. R. Craig, A. J. Kurdila, *Fundamentals of Structural Dynamics*, 2nd ed., Wiley, 2006.
- NAFEMS, *Selected Benchmarks for Forced Vibration* (R0016), test 5H: deep simply supported beam, harmonic forced vibration.

title: Investigate fillet-stress convergence of the automatic octree route
body:
## Current behaviour

The linear-static benchmark prepared for #875 shows that an accepted hex mesh can give an accurate global displacement while its recovered fillet stress remains outside the existing Tet10 reference band.

This is the repository's own SolidCraft filleted L-bracket: 8 mm leg thickness, 40 mm width, R6 inside fillet, two Ø8 holes. Steel has E = 210,000 MPa and ν = 0.3; `F2:side:l1` is fixed and a total 2,000 N x force is distributed over `F2:side:l5`, as in the existing fillet-stress oracle. The metric is the largest recovered nodal von Mises stress on `F3:blend:F2:side:l3|F2:side:l4`.

The existing 213 MPa reference is an internal four-level Tet10 convergence study, with a 3% band. It is not experimental validation or an exact stress solution. None of the reference values or accepted fixtures were changed for this comparison.

| Method | Requested size | Elements | Free equations | Mean tip ux | Fillet peak | Difference from 213 MPa |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| Tet10 | 8 mm | 14,384 | 71,970 | 0.151532 mm | 211.38 MPa | −0.76% |
| Tet10 | 6 mm | 14,907 | 74,370 | 0.151414 mm | 215.62 MPa | +1.23% |
| Tet10 | 4 mm | 18,577 | 92,148 | 0.151500 mm | 211.17 MPa | −0.86% |
| Octree Hex8I | 8 mm | 7,818 | 26,232 | 0.150239 mm | 192.68 MPa | −9.54% |
| Octree Hex8I | 6 mm | 7,818 | 26,232 | 0.150239 mm | 192.68 MPa | −9.54% |
| Octree Hex8I | 4 mm | 21,526 | 70,374 | 0.150607 mm | 198.06 MPa | −7.01% |

All hex meshes passed the requested all-Hex8, minimum scaled Jacobian 0.2 and maximum edge ratio 100 checks. Hex8I is FieldCraft's full-integration element with nine locally condensed incompatible modes. At 4 mm, mean tip displacement differs by only **0.59%** from the finest Tet10 result, while fillet stress remains **7.01% low** against the numerical reference. Both x reactions balance the 2 kN load to rounding.

The 8 and 6 mm requests give the same octree mesh; these are **two distinct hex resolutions**, not three independent refinement levels. The default force command divides the total over the selected face's nodes, so the discrete load distribution changes with each mesh. Both details must be controlled when investigating the difference.

## What you need and why

Users asking whether fewer hexes give faster, equally accurate FEA need a stress-convergence result, in addition to displacement, mesh validity and solve timing. The current data supports a displacement comparison but does not support an equal-stress-accuracy speedup claim.

## Reproduction

On the working benchmark branch associated with #875 (unpublished infrastructure; the tested automatic route resolves to the existing `mesh.hex.octree` mesher):

```sh
cargo run -p fieldcraft-engine --example volume_auto_fea -- bracket hex8i 4
cargo run -p fieldcraft-engine --example volume_auto_fea -- bracket tet10 4
```

Both use the original recipe at `tests/oracle/filleted-bracket-fillet-stress/design.json`, 0.05 mm tessellation tolerance, identical named faces and total force. Tet10 curvature angle is 32°. Caps are 90,000 source tets/hexes, 12,000 Steiner points, 300,000 DOFs and 120,000,000 factor entries. The runner prints the mesh reply, formulation, factor entries, three solve repetitions, reactions and stress metric. Compilation and design replay are excluded from recorded timings.

## Expected behaviour / investigation criteria

- [ ] Establish at least three **distinct** hex resolutions around the R6 fillet, recording actual element size/quality, geometry error and cost. Retain capped/failed attempts in the report.
- [ ] Separate geometric approximation, local resolution, linear-element distortion/formulation, stress extrapolation/averaging and the load-distribution effect. A maximum recovered nodal stress can move differently from stress at fixed physical stations; record both where appropriate.
- [ ] Establish a stable refined reference and explain whether the remaining difference is discretization error, the metric or an implementation defect. Preserve the provenance of the existing 213 MPa reference; do not change fixtures merely to hide the discrepancy.
- [ ] Demonstrate the proposed remedy at a stated stress and displacement target, with free equations, factor entries, meshing time and complete solve time compared with Tet10.
- [ ] Document the remaining limitation if the target cannot be reached within the stated caps. Mesh-quality acceptance must not be presented to agents as an FEA-error bound.

This is a follow-up investigation, not evidence that the existing octree oracle fails or that a solver regression has been identified. The benchmark and raw data in the #875 PR preserve the observations.

## References and provenance

- [Existing bracket model and convergence study](https://github.com/tangency-labs/fieldcraft/blob/develop/tests/oracle/filleted-bracket-fillet-stress/README.md).
- [Existing 213 MPa reference and tolerance](https://github.com/tangency-labs/fieldcraft/blob/develop/tests/oracle/filleted-bracket-fillet-stress/expected.json).
- [Element formulations and bending verification](https://github.com/tangency-labs/fieldcraft/blob/develop/docs/manual/structural/elements.md): Wilson et al. (1973), Taylor, Beresford and Wilson (1976).
- [Verification policy](https://github.com/tangency-labs/fieldcraft/blob/develop/docs/verification.md).

Geometry and all numerical results are generated by our SolidCraft/FieldCraft code. No commercial CAE software or GPL-family implementation was used. The benchmark changes no solver numerics or oracle fixtures.

title: General hex-dominant meshing: implementation strategy and validation
body:
## Status and scope

**Research and acceptance-definition issue. General hex-dominant meshing is not implemented or validated by the current work. No feature-completion PR has been published.**

The exploratory code selects existing structured/octree routes, checks explicit requirements, provides atomic retry replies, and includes a restricted six-Tet4 fan recombiner. This is useful infrastructure. It does not deliver the general mixed-mesh capability users may expect from the literature. Renaming the dispatcher does not implement the missing algorithm.

The proposed infrastructure name is **automatic volume meshing with a hex preference** (`mesh.volume.auto` in the working branch). A separately scoped infrastructure PR could be reviewed later; it would not close the general meshing objective here.

## Reference capability and implementation gap

The user's concrete reference is Ray, Sokolov, Reberol, Ledoux and Lévy, [*Hex-dominant meshing: Mind the gap!*](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.cad.2018.04.012), Computer-Aided Design 102:94–103 (2018), [HAL hal-01927557](https://inria.hal.science/hal-01927557/file/hexdom.pdf). This is distinct from Sokolov et al.'s 2016 paper.

| Capability | Current working implementation |
|---|---|
| Volume-wide parameterization for generating hexes | Not implemented |
| Extracted hexes and compatible quad-dominant object boundary | Not implemented |
| Residual cavity construction/remeshing with compatibility and geometric-error controls | Not implemented as that pipeline |
| Structured recognition and octree fitting | Existing meshers selected by the dispatcher |
| Tet-to-hex recombination | Only convex, exactly planar-faced six-tet fans with compatible Pyramid5 joins; broad mixed-CAD coverage is unproven |

The reference's robust completion is not a universal high-hex-percentage guarantee: poor fields can leave many tetrahedra. Tet fallback alone therefore does **not** disqualify a hex-dominant method. The substantive gaps are general hex generation, compatible boundary/cavity handling and realistic mixed-mesh evidence. Neither renaming nor a 50% acceptance gate fills them.

The checked primary definitions do not establish a universal 50%-by-volume threshold. Any threshold must be stated as FieldCraft policy or a caller requirement. Report element-count and volume fractions separately.

## What the existing evidence establishes

The 47-body diagnostic selection from our SolidCraft examples produced 28 accepted all-hex meshes versus 26 baseline passes under identical all-Hex8, minimum scaled Jacobian 0.2 and maximum edge ratio 100 criteria. Those 28 use **17 extrusions, 3 sweeps and 8 octree meshes**. Nineteen requests remain unmet; all 26 baseline passes remained passes. These are routing/acceptance results, not general mixed hex-dominant generation.

The sensor lid improved from 924 rejected standard-partition hexes (minimum SJ 0.164, edge ratio 85,310) to 580 accepted alternate-partition hexes (SJ 0.342, ratio 4.84) without relaxing thresholds. A headless MCP client completed the retry. The other improved bracket required **more** octree elements to meet quality.

The historical routing [source snapshot](https://github.com/takuto-NA/fieldcraft/tree/8267d9b7af563917b09ee317f299131e2a4af2d0) predates the naming correction and last upstream smooth-face rebase. It is not a released or completed general capability.

### Does fewer elements mean faster, equally accurate FEA?

No such general conclusion follows. On our controlled 200 × 20 × 20 mm bending beam, at the same 80 × 8 × 8 partition:

| Method | Elements | Free equations | Factor entries | Median complete solve | Tip error against Timoshenko theory |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| Tet4 | 30,720 | 19,440 | 5,387,985 | 718 ms | 5.14% |
| Ordinary Hex8 | 5,120 | 19,440 | 6,246,216 | 906 ms | 0.78% |

Six times fewer elements leaves nodes/free equations unchanged here. On the coarse beam, 10 incompatible-mode Hex8 (Hex8I) give 0.35% displacement error with 120 equations; 60 Tet10 give 0.15% with 540. Ordinary Hex8 is 33.4% too stiff. Formulation and convergence matter.

For our filleted bracket at requested size 4 mm, Hex8I mean tip displacement is within 0.59% of the finest Tet10 result, but fillet peak stress is 198.06 MPa, 7.01% below the existing internal 213 MPa reference and outside its 3% band. Tet10's three levels meet that band. **#876** tracks the investigation. The reference is an own-solver convergence study, not experimental or exact ground truth. Mesh quality is not an FEA-error bound.

These original linear-static measurements use CPU/f64, one solver thread, a Core Ultra 7 258V, Windows 11 and the repository development profile. Each row has one warm-up and three complete solves; compilation and initial CAD replay are excluded. Geometry, named constraints and total loads are specified consistently; the mesh-dependent nodal force distribution remains a documented limitation. Full convergence data is retained in the working benchmark.

## Acceptance before claiming general hex-dominant support

- [ ] Define supported inputs, chosen published methods and the exact output contract. The paper is a reference, not permission to imply identical guarantees.
- [ ] Implement at least one general hex-generating strategy, such as field/parameterization/aligned-point generation, and the boundary/residual-region handling it needs. A route selector or narrow fan matcher alone does not establish this milestone.
- [ ] Demonstrate realistic **mixed** meshes on our own non-sweepable SolidCraft geometries, rather than only synthetic lattice fans or existing all-hex routes. Publish count/volume fractions, cell types and actual backends.
- [ ] Verify certified validity, shared-face conformity, boundary/feature error, volume/topology preservation, adversarial geometry, determinism and bounded work. Retain failures/caps and preserve the previous model on rejection.
- [ ] Compare FEA convergence and time at stated displacement/stress targets against Tet10 as well as Tet4, with reactions, free equations, factor entries and complete mesh/solve cost. Keep #876 visible.
- [ ] Audit exact implementation/dependency licences and original assets. Publish a capability PR only after its stated scope is demonstrated.

## References and clean-room boundaries

The 2018 paper uses TetGen for cavity filling; it cannot be adopted under [FieldCraft's dependency rules](https://github.com/tangency-labs/fieldcraft/blob/develop/docs/adr/0001-libraries.md). A corresponding stage needs our own permitted implementation and verified boundary requirements. A paper's availability or a permissive wrapper does not license a forbidden dependency. No GPL-family source was read for this investigation.

Current exploratory volume-meshing code is original Rust under MIT OR Apache-2.0; existing SolidCraft/truck geometry dependencies are permissively licensed. No commercial CAD/CAE product produced these models, meshes or results. No paper figures or public CAD datasets are imported: tests use our own original reproducible geometry.

Additional primary references: [Pietroni et al.'s survey](https://doi.org/10.1145/3554920), [Pellerin et al.'s broader tet-to-hex identification method](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.cad.2018.05.004). The implemented six-tet search is a restricted subset of the latter's candidate/compatibility ideas.

title: Parameter studies over model inputs with tabulated derived results
body:
## Current behaviour

Comparing designs (fin spacing, inlet velocity, fan choice, heat load) means editing the model and re-solving by hand
for each value, then collecting the numbers manually.

## What to build

A **parameter study**:
- Choose one or more model parameters: a dimension from the geometry or an input such as inlet velocity, power or a
  material choice.
- Give a list or range of values. Each point solves in turn, or in parallel where resources allow, with the usual solve
  caps.
- Each point records the derived results from #837 (heat rate, pressure drop, outlet temperatures, maximum solid temperature)
  and the validity and acceptance report.
- Output is a table and CSV, plus an XY plot of any result against the parameter.
- A failed or invalid point is shown as such and doesn't stop the study.

## Verification

- A study over the inlet velocity of a heated channel: the recorded heat rate and pressure drop match individual
  solves.
- A forced failure at one point is reported and the rest complete.

Part of #697; the fin-spacing comparison in #701 relies on it.

title: Guided setup for conjugate heat-transfer models
body:
## Current behaviour

A heat-transfer model with flow and solids is built from several separate commands:
- fluid domain;
- fluid material;
- obstacle bodies and their solid materials;
- inlets, outlets and walls;
- heat sources and thermal faces;
- a fluid step and its settings.

It's easy to miss a piece, and new users don't know the order.

## What to build

A guided setup that walks through those steps in order, with sensible defaults and a check at the end:
1. Pick the bodies that are fluid regions and the bodies that are solids.
2. Assign materials, from the library (#838) or custom.
3. Mark inlets (velocity or flow rate, temperature), outlets and walls.
4. Add heat sources (power per body) and thermal faces.
5. Choose the resolution, with a cell-count and run-time estimate before solving.
6. Run the model check, then offer to solve.

Every step is an ordinary command, so a script can do the same thing. The guided setup only sequences them and never
does anything a command can't. It can also start from a saved example, such as the electronics or exchanger samples.

## Verification

- A scripted run of the setup produces the same model as the equivalent command sequence.
- The final check catches each missing piece: no inlet, no material, unpowered solids, and an over-cap cell count.

Part of #697; supports the tutorials in #701.

title: Thermal and fluid material library with temperature-dependent properties
body:
## Current behaviour

The material library (#99) covers structural metals. Thermal material properties are listed as coming soon. Heat
transfer between flow and solids needs, for every model:
- the fluid's density, viscosity, conductivity and specific heat;
- the solid's conductivity, specific heat and density.

Users currently type these in by hand.

## What to build

Library entries with cited sources (handbook or standard reference data, with the citation in the entry and a row in
the attribution list where required):
- **Fluids:** water, air, and a common water/glycol coolant mix. Properties are temperature-dependent over a stated
  range, as a table or fit, with the valid range enforced or warned about.
- **Solids:** aluminium alloys (e.g. 6061, 6063), copper, carbon and stainless steel, brass, FR-4 (orthotropic
  conductivity), borosilicate and silica glass, and a typical thermal interface material.

Entries can be picked with one click in the material dialog and by name in commands. A model saves the values it used,
so results don't change if the library is updated.

## Verification

- Each entry's values match its cited source at tabulated points.
- Interpolation inside the range and the warning outside it are tested.
- A natural-convection oracle case gives the same answer with library air as with hand-entered values.

Part of #697.

title: Derived heat-exchanger results: heat rate, face averages, pressure drop, duty and energy balance
body:
## Current behaviour

Fluid results can be shown as slices, streamlines and signed wall heat per area, but there are no commands for the
numbers a heat-exchanger study reports. The exchanger tutorials in #701 assume them.

## What to build

Read-only results commands, available from the GUI, CLI, scripts and the control channel:
- **Heat rate** through a named face set or surface (W), split into conduction and advection where meaningful.
- **Face averages** at a named face: area-averaged and mass-flow-weighted temperature, and area-averaged pressure and
  velocity.
- **Mass and volume flow** through a face.
- **Pressure drop** between two named faces.
- **Exchanger summary:** for a hot and a cold stream, the heat duty, both inlet and outlet temperatures, effectiveness
  and log-mean temperature difference.
- **Energy balance:** heat in through inlets, faces and sources against heat out, plus storage, with the residual as a
  fraction. This shows whether a result is converged and closed.

Results come as a table and CSV, with units, and say which time window they average over for unsteady runs. They are
reported as measurements, not validation.

## Verification

- A heated channel with analytic heat input: the energy balance closes to the stated tolerance, and outlet mean
  temperature matches the energy balance.
- Poiseuille flow: the pressure drop matches the analytic value.
- Synthetic fields with known integrals.

Part of #697; used by #701.

title: Thin conducting walls and internal baffles between fluid regions
body:
## Current behaviour

A conducting wall between two fluid regions has to be a voxelised solid, so its thickness has to be resolved by
lattice cells. Real heat-exchanger walls (tube walls, plate fins, separator sheets) are 0.1–1 mm thick, while the
passages either side are millimetres to centimetres wide. Resolving the wall sets the cell size for the whole domain.
For the coupled air/coolant exchanger in #700, that makes the run far more expensive than the flow needs.

## What to build

A **thin wall** (baffle): a zero-thickness sheet defined on a face set or surface, placed inside a fluid domain.
- **Flow:** it acts as a no-slip (or slip) wall on both sides, separating the passages either side. Fluid can't cross
  it.
- **Heat:** it conducts through its thickness with a user-given thickness and conductivity (or a conductance per area,
  W/m²K), plus optional in-plane conduction along the sheet.
- **Results:** temperature and heat flux are reported separately on each side, so the side-to-side difference is
  visible.
- **Coupling:** it works with the existing conducting solids, component power and thermal contact resistance (#677),
  and on both the CPU and GPU paths, or refuses clearly where unsupported.

## Verification

- A plane wall between two counter-flowing channels: overall heat-transfer coefficient and outlet temperatures against
  the analytic two-stream solution.
- The same wall resolved as a voxelised solid at high resolution, matched within a stated tolerance.
- Zero conductance must give zero heat crossing the wall to round-off.

Part of the heat-exchanger workflow in #697; needed for #700.

title: [Feature Request] Modern, workflow-first UI/UX inspired by SimScale
body:
### Current behaviour

FieldCraft is an incredibly promising project, and I genuinely appreciate the ambition to create a fully open-source, local-first engineering simulation platform.

However, in my opinion, its current interface still follows many of the traditional design conventions found throughout engineering simulation software.

This isn't exclusively an open-source problem. Even expensive, industry-standard CAE applications often rely on dated interface conventions, dense toolbars, deeply nested menus, and workflows that feel unnecessarily complicated by modern software design standards.

I recognize that FieldCraft has already received substantial UI/UX improvements, including those introduced in v0.6. My suggestion concerns the broader visual design philosophy and overall user experience, rather than any single missing feature or usability bug.

One example of a different approach is SimScale, which demonstrates how sophisticated engineering software can be presented through a cleaner, more modern, and visually coherent interface.

### What you need and why

I'd love to see FieldCraft explore a more ambitious, workflow-oriented UI/UX direction, taking inspiration from modern simulation platforms such as [[SimScale](https://www.simscale.com/)](https://www.simscale.com/).

As an aerospace engineering student, I believe that an intuitive, visually polished simulation environment can significantly improve both accessibility and productivity.

What makes SimScale particularly appealing to me isn't simply its appearance. It's the way the interface organizes complex engineering tasks into understandable workflows, maintains a clear visual hierarchy, and makes advanced functionality approachable without sacrificing technical depth.

I believe FieldCraft has an opportunity to go beyond matching the capabilities or interfaces of existing commercial software. It could help establish a new standard for how engineering simulation applications should look, feel, and function.

A genuinely modern multiphysics application could appeal not only to students and hobbyists but also to professional engineers who are accustomed to powerful software with outdated user experiences.

Since FieldCraft is still relatively early in its development, I think this could be an excellent opportunity to explore a more distinctive design direction.

I completely understand that the maintainers may have different priorities or a different vision for the project. I'm proposing this as a long-term design discussion, not an expectation or demand for an immediate redesign.

### Expected behaviour

Rather than simply refreshing icons or changing colors, I'd love to see FieldCraft explore a more comprehensive, workflow-first user interface.

Some ideas worth considering:

**1. Modern visual design**
- A clean, cohesive design language with consistent typography, spacing, and visual hierarchy.
- Carefully designed light and dark themes.
- Less visual clutter, with greater emphasis on simulation geometry and results.
- Contextual controls that appear when relevant rather than displaying every available operation simultaneously.
- Modern, responsive panels and dialogs.

**2. Guided simulation workflows**
- An intuitive process for creating a simulation, selecting physics, assigning materials, generating meshes, configuring boundary conditions, solving, and reviewing results.
- Clear visual indicators showing which setup stages are complete, incomplete, or contain errors.
- Progressive disclosure of advanced settings so beginners aren't immediately overwhelmed.
- Sensible defaults, while preserving access to advanced controls.

**3. More interactive 3D visualization**
- A large, central viewport that remains the focus of the application.
- Direct interaction with geometry, faces, boundaries, materials, and loads.
- Context-sensitive property panels linked to selections in the viewport.
- Smooth transitions between geometry, mesh, and simulation results.
- Clear, polished visualization of stress, deformation, pressure, temperature, and other physical quantities.

**4. Unified simulation management**
- A visually organized project dashboard.
- Easy comparison between different simulations and configurations.
- Clear simulation progress, convergence monitoring, and solver diagnostics.
- Convenient access to previous results without navigating through numerous technical menus.

**Closing thoughts**

I'm not suggesting that FieldCraft should copy SimScale's proprietary interface. Rather, I think SimScale provides an excellent example of the level of visual polish, accessibility, and workflow clarity that modern engineering applications can achieve.

It would be great to see FieldCraft explore its own distinctive interpretation of these principles.

Even a design exploration, community discussion, or a few alternative UI mockups could be valuable.

**Would the maintainers be open to considering a more substantial UI/UX redesign inspired by modern simulation platforms as a longer-term goal?**

Thank you for your work on FieldCraft and for making such an ambitious project open source!

### Pictures

_No response_

### References

[FieldCraft's existing roadmap](https://github.com/tangency-labs/fieldcraft/blob/develop/ROADMAP.md?utm_source=chatgpt.com) — acknowledgement of current UI/UX development.

title: Feature Request: Official Docker Image with Browser-Accessible GUI

I currently use SolidCraft through Docker Compose, which allows users to access the application through a web browser without installing the desktop application on each PC.

- **Consistent environments:** All users can work with the same application version and runtime environment.

Based on my experience with SolidCraft, I believe this would make FieldCraft much easier to deploy, maintain, and share within a community or organization.

- An official Docker image that includes the FieldCraft GUI.

title: FDM parts: take the layer direction from SolidCraft's print face, and report the stress across the layers
body:
### What are you trying to do

I check 3D-printed (FDM) parts. Their weak direction is across the layers: the tensile strength between layers is often a third to a half of the in-plane value. So the first question for a printed part is how much tension crosses the layers, and whether printing it on another face would help.

SolidCraft stores the face a body prints on (Print face, since 0.28.0: `print_faces` in the design, by body name). The build direction is therefore already in the design FieldCraft opens, but FieldCraft doesn't read it. Today I note which way each part prints and work out the stress along that direction by hand, which is only easy when the build direction is a global axis (`stress_zz`).

### How I imagine it working

In three steps, each useful without the next:

1. **Read the print face.** When a body of the opened design has a print face, `inspect_model` lists that body's **build direction**: the normal of the print face, the direction the layers stack in. A `build_direction` vector can also be given by hand. Without either, nothing changes.
2. **A result field and a check.** `results.contour {"field": "stress_across_layers"}` is the normal stress along the build direction (n · σ · n) of a static step, with its largest tensile value in the reply. A check, "across-layer tension ≤ allowable", gives pass or fail and the margin. This needs no new material model: with an isotropic material it's already the usual first check.
3. **Material orientation from it, once orientations exist.** Orthotropic elastic materials exist (`engineering_constants`), but their axes are the global ones until material orientations land (Sections › Orientation is "coming soon (M8)" in `docs/features.md`). When they do, "from the print face" would be one more way to set one, with the material's third axis along the build direction. A few named starting points for common filaments (PLA, PETG, ASA, PET-CF at 100 % infill) could come with it, marked as rough values to replace with coupon data.

### Why

It turns the most common printed-part failure check into one step, and it uses data SolidCraft already saves. It also catches the classic mistake of printing a part on the wrong face: change the print face and solve again.

### Notes

Edited 2026-11-18 after checking against develop: the first version said I set up an orthotropic material along the build direction today, which isn't possible yet without material orientations, so the request is now split so that steps 1 and 2 don't wait for them. No command or result on develop mentions a print face or a build direction. Step 1 reads one more section of the design; step 2 is post-processing of the stress FieldCraft already stores.

🤖 Generated with [Claude Code](https://claude.com/claude-code)

title: Translate the desktop app's interface, starting with French
body:
### Current behaviour

The interface is English-only. Every label is an English string in the code: about 1,000 in `crates/ui-egui` (menus, panels, buttons, tooltips, status messages), plus the 170 command labels and the form fields' labels, hints and help in `crates/engine` (`CommandSpec.label`, `schema::Field`, the ribbon catalogue). There is no message catalogue and no language setting, so an engineer can't use FieldCraft in their own language.

### What you need and why

Many engineers, students and teaching labs in France, Belgium, Switzerland, Quebec and French-speaking Africa work in French. A pre-processor is full of domain terms (sets, sections, steps, loads, boundary conditions, result quantities), and a translated interface makes FieldCraft much easier to teach and adopt there. SolidCraft already ships a French interface, so a part opened from SolidCraft lands today in a FieldCraft that only speaks English. #734 also asks for documentation "available in the languages required for its intended markets"; this issue covers the app's interface only.

I'd like to do this work myself. Because it touches most of `ui-egui`, I'd rather agree on the approach with you before writing any code.

### Expected behaviour

- A **Language** preference (`files::Prefs`): `system` by default (the OS locale on desktop, `navigator.languages` on the web), or a language chosen from the list. Untranslated messages fall back to English.
- **Only what's shown is translated.** Command ids, parameter keys, JSON replies, CLI output, the MCP tools, control-channel replies, file formats, unit symbols and user names stay exactly as they are, so scripts, agents and decks never depend on the UI language. Tests and scenarios always run in English, so they read the same text on every machine.
- **Guarded coverage**, as SolidCraft does: tests fail when a command label, ribbon tab/panel or menu label is missing from the English catalogue, and a report lists what each language is still missing.
- **An original French catalogue** with a short glossary for translators. Some French words cover several English ones: *contrainte* is both *stress* and *constraint*, *pas* can be a time increment or a step, *étape* is an analysis step, and *chargement* a load or a loading history. Each meaning needs its own entry and a note. No wording is taken from commercial CAE products' localised interfaces; the translation is written from FieldCraft's English text.

Suggested slicing, each part its own PR and each commit building and passing its tests:
1. The catalogue mechanism, the language preference, system-locale matching and the coverage tests, with English alone (no visible change).
2. The `ui-egui` texts and the engine's display labels go through the catalogue (still no visible change in English).
3. `fr.json`, the glossary, and before/after screenshots.

### Questions for the maintainer

1. **Which mechanism?** There are two candidates in the Craft family:
   - SolidCraft's `crates/ui-egui/src/i18n.rs`: per-app JSON catalogues in `assets/locales/`, keyed by stable ids plus an adapter from engine labels, and documented in `docs/localization.md`. It would be adapted under MIT OR Apache-2.0 and noted in ATTRIBUTION.md.
   - The shared `craft-i18n` crate in `storytold/craft-libs`: shared and per-app catalogues, plurals, number formatting, system locale. FieldCraft already depends on craft-libs, but at a revision that predates this crate, so the pin would move and it brings ICU4X dependencies (licence and wasm checks via `deny.toml`/`cargo xtask wasm`).
2. **Engine labels:** translate them in the UI from `cmd.<command id>` keys, which leaves `CommandSpec` untouched (my preference), or change the engine's types?
3. **Scope:** French alone at first, with the mechanism open to other languages later?

### Pictures

Screenshots of the ribbon, a command form and the results panel in French will be in the last PR.

### References

- SolidCraft `docs/localization.md` and `crates/ui-egui/src/i18n.rs` (tangency-labs/solidcraft)
- `storytold/craft-libs` `crates/i18n/README.md`
- Unicode CLDR language matching (BCP 47 tags, fallback from a region to its base language)

title: lbm-gpu: the throughput benchmarks fail in parallel on NVIDIA with "the readback did not complete"
body:
### Observed failure

The `lbm-gpu` throughput benchmarks (`crates/lbm-gpu/tests/throughput.rs`, all `#[ignore]`d, so part of `cargo xtask test --heavy`) fail now and then on a real NVIDIA card when they run in parallel, the default for `cargo test`:

```
thread 'smagorinsky_cost' panicked at crates/lbm-gpu/tests/throughput.rs:312:40:
called `Result::unwrap()` on an `Err` value: Backend("GPU: the readback did not complete")
thread 'cell_updates_per_second' panicked at crates/lbm-gpu/tests/throughput.rs:121:28:
called `Result::unwrap()` on an `Err` value: Backend("GPU: the readback did not complete")
```

`zone_throughput_and_diagnostic_cost` failed once as well (at `throughput.rs:54`, `device.advance(32).unwrap()`).

### Reproduction

```
FIELDCRAFT_GPU=hardware FIELDCRAFT_REQUIRE_GPU=1 \
  cargo test --profile ci -p fieldcraft-lbm-gpu --test throughput -- --include-ignored
```

Repeated on the same machine, `develop` at cb97611:

| | runs | failed with "the readback did not complete" |
|---|---|---|
| default test threads | 12 | 4 (1–2 tests each); one more run ended without any test result, its output was not kept |
| `--test-threads=1` | 1 | 0 |
| `smagorinsky_cost` alone | 2 | 0 |

### Evidence

No Xid in the guest's kernel log, no PCIe/AER messages on the host, the card idle at 41 °C afterwards. `verification.rs` and the other tests of the crate pass in the same runs.

### Expected behaviour

The benchmarks pass, as they do one at a time. CI runs them on lavapipe only, so it does not see this.

### Investigation

`verification.rs` takes a shared turn (`static TURN: Mutex<()>`, #616) since the parallel hang in #614 (NVIDIA, concurrent devices); `throughput.rs` does not, so its six benchmarks share the card. The error comes from `read` in `crates/lbm-gpu/src/native.rs`: `device.poll(PollType::Wait { .. })` returns `Ok`, but the `map_async` callback has not run yet, so `rx.try_recv()` is empty. The runs end in about 60 s, well inside `DEVICE_TIMEOUT` (120 s). I have not looked further into why the poll returns before the callback. Taking the same turn in `throughput.rs` would also keep the measured rates clean (in parallel they read 837 M cell updates/s against 1115–1686 M/s alone).

### Version and platform

`develop` at cb97611 (0.7.0). NVIDIA GeForce RTX 3060 Ti, NVIDIA open kernel module 615.78.08, Vulkan, power-limited to 186 W, passed through to a Fedora 44 x86_64 KVM guest (kernel 7.2.14).

title: Staircase geometry: drag depends on how many cells span the body and on where it sits on the grid (periodic Stokes sphere +11.7 % at R = 3 cells; Schäfer–Turek C_d,max +6.7 % at D/Δx 20 and −8.5 % on a half-cell shift)
body:
Part of the LES accuracy and stability tracking issue (#785). ## Observed Obstacles are voxelised (a cell is solid when its centre is inside the body) and bounded by halfway bounce-back, so a curved body is a staircase of lattice faces. Two steady or laminar controls on develop `cb976117` quantify what that costs in drag, independently of any turbulence model: **Periodic array of Stokes spheres** (theory: Hasimoto 1959 with Sangani & Acrivos 1982's higher terms, K = 2.0215 at volume fraction 0.0276): | Sphere radius | Box | K measured | vs theory | |---|---|---|---| | 3 cells | 16³ | 2.2572 | **+11.66 %** | | 6 cells | 32³ | 2.0550 | +1.66 % | Mass is conserved to roundoff and the wall force equals the driving force at steady state in both, so the error is geometric, not a force-accounting error. **Confined cylinder, Schäfer & Turek Re 100 (2D-2Z, scaled to D = 1), TRT, lattice velocity 0.05:** | Grid / change | Mean C_d ± 95 % half-width | C_d,max | vs 3.22–3.24 | St (ref. 0.295–0.305) | Outcome | |---|---|---|---|---|---| | D/Δx = 20, τ 0.52, CPU | 3.34682 ± 0.00031 | 3.44664 | **+6.7 %** | 0.29870 (periods 0.29837–0.29891) | stable 120 D/U | | Same, GPU f32 | 3.346814 ± 0.000306 | 3.44659 | +6.7 % | 0.298703 | CPU/GPU C_d differ by 7 × 10⁻⁵ % | | D/Δx = 20, regularized | 3.37737 ± 0.00046 | 3.49203 | +8.1 % | 0.29746 | collision changes C_d by +0.9 % | | D/Δx = 20, body shifted +0.5 cell in y | 3.10202 ± 0.00039 | 3.15345 | **−2.4 %** | 0.30442 | mean −7.3 %, peak −8.5 % from unshifted | | D/Δx = 10, τ 0.51 | invalid | — | — | — | unstable at 91.4 D/U (CPU), 47.6 D/U (GPU): lattice speed 0.66 | A half-cell shift of the body moves the peak drag by 8.5 % at 20 cells per diameter. (The shift also moves the body 0.025 D in the 4.1 D channel, so it is a combined placement sensitivity, not a pure grid-phase error; the solver has no way to translate the grid under fixed physical boundaries.) For the LES cases the implication is that 12–24 cells per diameter (the resolutions the SGS τ floor admits at Re 3900) carry a geometric drag error of the same order as the terms being studied, and that the N = 8 quasi-2D runs with the body shifted half a cell (C_d 2.29 against 1.87 unshifted on the GPU, +22 %) cannot be read as a wall-placement effect at all because both drift by about 0.9 between window halves. Setup refusals bound the other end: at Re 300 000, N = 16 and lattice velocity 0.05 the setup is refused ("τ = 0.50001 is below 0.5001 … cell Reynolds number 18750"); the SGS floor alone would need D/Δx ≥ 200 there, and without SGS the 0.505 floor would need D/Δx ≥ 130 at Re 3900. Those are stability policy limits, not accuracy limits: satisfying the SGS floor admits grids with well under one cell across the boundary layer. ## Reproduce (from develop) Stokes sphere array (CPU, about 25 s): ```sh cargo test --release -p fieldcraft-lbm --test verification stokes_drag_of_a_sphere_array_matches_hasimoto -- --ignored --nocapture ``` (periodic box, ν = 5/6 so τ = 3 with Λ = 3/16, body acceleration 10⁻⁶, sphere `sphere(centre, r, 4)`, 1500 / 3000 steps; the test passes because it only asserts that refinement improves and that R = 6 is within 5 %.) Schäfer–Turek recipes (CPU; the Mach row on GPU): ```json {"id":"sch100-n20-trt","shape":"sch100","cells":20,"end":120,"start":80} {"id":"sch100-n10-trt","shape":"sch100","cells":10,"end":120,"start":80} {"id":"sch100-n20-rr","shape":"sch100","cells":20,"collision":"regularized","end":120,"start":80} {"id":"sch100-n20-offset","shape":"sch100","cells":20,"offset":0.5,"end":120,"start":80} ``` Setup: box 22 D × 4.1 D × one cell, cylinder of radius 0.5 D centred at (2 D, 2 D) (+0.5 cell in y for the shifted row), `x_min` velocity [1.5, 0, 0] with `"profile": "parabolic"`, `x_max` pressure 0 uniform, `y_min`/`y_max` walls, `z_min`/`z_max` periodic, ν = 0.01, TRT Λ = 3/16 (or regularized), no turbulence, Δt = 0.05 Δx / 1.5, 120 D/U, statistics over 80–120 D/U, C_d = 2 F_x / (ρ U² D · span) with U = 1 the mean inlet velocity. Reference: Schäfer & Turek (1996), doi:10.1007/978-3-322-89849-4_39. Drag-crisis refusal (GPU, instant): ```json {"id":"crisis300000-n16-refusal","shape":"cylinder","re":300000,"cells":16,"cs":0.1,"collision":"hrr","end":10,"start":5} ```
Common external-flow setup used by every bluff-body case below (click to expand) All bluff-body cases are nondimensional: D = U = ρ = 1, ν = 1/Re. title: At the default lattice velocity 0.05 the Re 3900 cylinder develops ±5 % density excursions and a local Mach of 0.15; halving it cleans the field but leaves the drag at +38.6 %
body:
Part of the LES accuracy and stability tracking issue (#785). ## Observed The solver's automatic time step sets the characteristic lattice velocity to 0.05 (Ma 0.087), where the weakly compressible error is of order Ma² ≈ 0.75 %. In the LES bluff-body runs the local fields go well beyond that: | Case | Lattice velocity | τ | ρ range at the end | Local Ma at the end | Mean C_d (100–200 D/U) | vs 0.99 | |---|---|---|---|---|---|---| | Cylinder Re 3900, N = 12, HRR | 0.05 (default) | 0.50046 | **0.954–1.050** | **0.154** | 1.3539 ± 0.0401 | +36.8 % | | Same, N = 16 | 0.05 | 0.50062 | 0.945–1.068 | 0.173 | 1.3227 ± 0.0254 | +33.6 % | | Same, N = 24 | 0.05 | 0.50092 | 0.945–1.073 | 0.170 | 1.3380 ± 0.0245 | +35.1 % | | Same, N = 12, lattice velocity halved | 0.025 | 0.50023 | 0.9966–1.0037 | 0.090 | 1.3724 ± 0.0524 | **+38.6 %** | | Same, N = 12, lattice velocity doubled | 0.1 | 0.50092 | 0.721–1.374 | 0.348 | 1.3672 ± 0.0710 | +38.1 % | | Square Re 22 000, N = 16, HRR | 0.05 | 0.50011 | 0.879–1.136 | 0.162 | 4.106 ± 0.140 | +95 % | Halving the lattice velocity reduces the density variation from about ±5 % to ±0.4 % and the C_l rms from 0.32 to 0.16, but the mean drag does not move toward the experiment (+1.4 % from baseline). Doubling it leaves the mean drag similar too, while the density spans 0.72–1.37. The drag excess is therefore not a compressibility error of the force statistic, and a mean C_d that is insensitive to Mach is not evidence that the compressibility is harmless: the fields say otherwise. The laminar control shows the expected direction: the Schäfer–Turek Re 100 case at N = 20 has C_d,max +6.7 % at lattice velocity 0.05 and +4.2 % at 0.025 (ρ 0.9990–1.0017), with St unchanged at 0.2987. Note that lowering the lattice velocity also lowers τ − ½ in proportion (τ − ½ = 3 u_lattice (D/Δx) / Re), so none of these is a pure compressibility change; the collision moves closer to its τ = ½ limit at the same time. ## Reproduce (from develop) Recipes (GPU): ```json {"id":"c3900-n12-hrr","shape":"cylinder","re":3900,"cells":12,"cs":0.1,"collision":"hrr","outlet":"convective","end":200,"start":100} {"id":"c3900-n12-hrr-ma025","shape":"cylinder","re":3900,"cells":12,"speed":0.025,"cs":0.1,"collision":"hrr","outlet":"convective","end":200,"start":100} {"id":"c3900-n12-hrr-ma100","shape":"cylinder","re":3900,"cells":12,"speed":0.1,"cs":0.1,"collision":"hrr","outlet":"convective","end":200,"start":100} {"id":"sch100-n20-trt","shape":"sch100","cells":20,"end":120,"start":80} {"id":"sch100-n20-ma025","shape":"sch100","cells":20,"speed":0.025,"end":120,"start":80} ``` In the common script the lattice velocity is set through `time_step`: 0.0041666667 (0.05), 0.0020833333 (0.025), 0.0083333333 (0.1) at N = 12. Read the final density field's minimum and maximum and the maximum |u|·√3 (local Ma) from the saved frame. The Schäfer–Turek control (`sch100`): box 22 D × 4.1 D × one cell, cylinder centred at (2 D, 2 D), parabolic inlet with peak 1.5 U (mean U), uniform pressure outlet, no-slip top and bottom, periodic span, Re = U D/ν = 100, TRT Λ = 3/16, no turbulence model, lattice velocity 0.05 at the inlet peak (τ = 0.52 at N = 20), 120 D/U with statistics over 80–120 D/U. title: Coarse TRT LES runs to completion with a negative mean drag (C_d −3.8 ± 4.5) and the guard never trips
body:
Part of the LES accuracy and stability tracking issue (#785). ## Observed A quasi-2D cylinder at Re 3900 with the TRT collision and Smagorinsky C_s 0.1 reaches its 160 D/U end without the runtime guard (lattice speed > 0.5 or non-positive density) firing, yet its force history is nonphysical: the mean drag over the averaging window is negative, with block means swinging between −9 and +8, and the lift rms is five times the body's projected area force scale. | Backend | Mean C_d ± 95 % half-width (80–160 D/U) | Block means | C_d,max | C_l rms | ρ range at the end | Local Ma | |---|---|---|---|---|---|---| | CPU f64 | **−3.844 ± 4.531** | −2.9, −8.1, +8.1, −3.9, −3.6, −9.0, −3.2, −8.1 | 15.1 | 5.16 | 0.989–1.007 | 0.158 | | GPU f32 | **−2.082 ± 5.554** | +7.6, −6.9, −11.1, +1.2, −2.6, −8.3, −2.3, +5.8 | 20.1 | 5.10 | 0.993–1.011 | 0.150 | The density stays within ±1 % and the lattice speed within the limit, so the guard sees a healthy run. The same case with HRR σ 0.99 gives a positive C_d of 1.87 ± 0.03 (both backends, explicit seed), and with MRT fails at step 599 (#790). The solver's own warning at setup for this case reads: "τ = 0.5003 is close to ½: under-resolved flows may go unstable; a finer spacing or the regularized collision is safer". title: MRT fails within the first D/U at every LES bluff-body setting tried (τ ≈ 0.5001–0.5005)
body:
Part of the LES accuracy and stability tracking issue (#785). ## Observed With the MRT collision and Smagorinsky C_s 0.1 at the molecular τ these cases need, the run goes unstable almost at once, on both backends, before any statistics can be taken. HRR at the same settings runs to the end. | Case | Backend | τ | Fails at step | Flow time | Reported trigger | |---|---|---|---|---|---| | Cylinder Re 3900, N = 12, 3D (3.1667 D span) | GPU | 0.50046 | 120 | 0.5 D/U | lattice speed 0.769 (limit 0.5) | | Same, divergence-free analytic start | GPU | 0.50046 | 144 | 0.6 D/U | lattice speed 5.7 × 10⁴ | | Cylinder Re 3900, N = 8, one-cell span | CPU f64 | 0.50031 | 599 | 3.7 D/U | lattice speed 0.560 | | Same | GPU f32 | 0.50031 | 816 | 5.1 D/U | lattice speed 0.505 | | Square Re 22 000, N = 16, 4 D span | GPU | 0.50011 | 128 | 0.4 D/U | lattice speed 1.5 × 10⁵ | The failure step differs between CPU and GPU on the quasi-2D case (599 vs 816), so the onset is precision-sensitive, but both backends fail. The manual already records that MRT with C_s 0.1 behaves badly in the wall-modelled channels (energy pile-up, "plug" profile) and that TRT in the Han A20 channel goes unstable at 0.4 δ/u_τ; this issue records the external-flow counterpart, where MRT does not survive at all. The collision rates are the fixed d'Humières et al. (2002) set (1.19, 1.4, 1.2, 1.98) with the five shear rates local. ## Reproduce (from develop) Recipes: ```json {"id":"c3900-n12-mrt","shape":"cylinder","re":3900,"cells":12,"cs":0.1,"collision":"mrt","outlet":"convective","end":200,"start":100} {"id":"c3900-n12-mrt-potential","shape":"cylinder","re":3900,"cells":12,"cs":0.1,"collision":"mrt","outlet":"convective","initial":"potential","end":200,"start":100} {"id":"c3900-n8-mrt-2d","shape":"cylinder","re":3900,"cells":8,"span":0.125,"cs":0.1,"collision":"mrt","outlet":"convective","end":160,"start":80} {"id":"square22000-n16-mrt","shape":"square","re":22000,"cells":16,"span":4,"height":14,"cs":0.1,"collision":"mrt","outlet":"convective","end":240,"start":120} ``` In the common script, `"collision": "mrt"` on the step; everything else as the baseline cylinder. The run ends with: ``` unstable: the flow went unstable by time step 120: the lattice speed reached 0.769 (limit 0.5) or a density stopped being a positive number; lower the time step, refine the spacing or check the boundary conditions ```

title: Square cylinder at Re 22 000: C_d 4.11 ± 0.14 against about 2.1, with force spikes to 24.8 and an unusable Strouhal number
body:
Part of the LES accuracy and stability tracking issue (#785). ## Observed A square cylinder LES at Re = 22 000 on develop `cb976117` finishes without tripping the stability guard, but its mean drag is roughly twice the measured value, its force history has large spikes, and no shedding frequency can be read from it. | Quantity | Measured (120–240 D/U) | Reference | |---|---|---| | Mean C_d ± 95 % half-width | **4.106 ± 0.140** | ≈ 2.1 (**+95 %**) | | C_d,max | 24.84 | — | | C_l rms | 0.90 | — | | Block lag-1 / half-window drift | 0.061 / +0.206 | — | | Raw lift-crossing frequency | 2.096 (periods 0.38–7.4 D/U) | St 0.132 ± 0.004 | | ρ range at the end | 0.879–1.136 | ±1 % would be expected at lattice Ma 0.087 | | Local Ma at the end | 0.162 | prescribed 0.087 | Reference: Lyn, Einav, Rodi & Park (1995), J. The square's faces lie on lattice planes at N = 16, so this case has **no curved-wall staircasing**; its error is larger than the circular cylinder's (+37 %), so staircasing is not a universal explanation of the drag excess.
